_about: Single source of truth for every rendering, and the auditable term ledger (check 5). ONE rendering per referent for the whole book. Before you romanize any name, check here. status per entry: 'attested' (form used in English scholarship, give the citation in note), 'provisional' (your romanization, not found in outside sources), 'decided' (a project style call). If you find a better attested form mid-book, change it here AND grep every built chapter for the old form, then rebuild. Sections are rendered as glossary headings; keys starting with '_' are ignored. Add/rename sections freely (people, organizations, places, terms, ...).

张小敬.note: The protagonist; a one-eyed former buliang chief of Wannian County, taken from the death cells. Pinyin.

李泌.note: Historical statesman (722–789), courtesy name Changyuan; here the young deputy director of the Jing’an Bureau. Pinyin follows the standard scholarly form; see D. Twitchett (ed.), The Cambridge History of China, vol. 3.

长源.note: Li Bi’s courtesy name (zi), by which Director He addresses him.

贺监.note: The white-haired official; jian is his post as Director of the Palace Library. The novel’s figure evokes the poet He Zhizhang (659–744), who held that title.

崔六郎.note: A West Market fixer; Liulang means ‘Sixth Son.’ Brother of Cui Qi. Pinyin.

崔器.note: Commander of the Lüben Guards; younger brother of Cui Liulang. Pinyin.

曹破延.note: A Turkic Wolf Guard posing as a Sogdian merchant from Kang. Pinyin.

徐宾.note: A recorder in the Jing’an Bureau, courtesy name Youde; a former Ministry of Revenue clerk with a prodigious memory. Pinyin.

姚汝能.note: A young clerk of the Jing’an Bureau. Pinyin.

檀棋.note: Li Bi’s maidservant, of mixed Han and Sogdian parentage, who works the sand-table. Pinyin.

乌苏米施可汗.note: Özmiş Qaghan (r. 742–744), last khagan of the Second Turkic Khaganate; historically killed by the Basmyl in 744. Form per M. R. Drompp and standard Turkological usage.

王忠嗣.note: Wang Zhongsi (705–749), Tang military commissioner of Shuofang. Pinyin per The Cambridge History of China, vol. 3.

张说.note: Zhang Yue (667–730), chief minister and Secretariat Director under Xuanzong; the surname’s literary reading is Yue. Pinyin per standard Tang scholarship.

颜真卿.note: Yan Zhenqing (709–785), one of the great masters of Chinese calligraphy; the Jing’an Bureau’s name-board is in his hand. Pinyin, standard.

孙思邈.note: Sun Simiao (traditionally 581–682), physician venerated as the Medicine King (Yaowang); the Jing’an Bureau occupies his former residence. Pinyin, standard.

闻染.note: A young incense-shop owner in the West Market whose father died the year before; protected by an unnamed benefactor. Pinyin.

封大伦.note: A middle-aged official in a blue robe who bears a grudge against Wen Ran and her late father. Pinyin.

岑参.note: Cen Shen (c. 715–770), one of the great Tang frontier poets. Appears here as a young man whose horse is stolen. The surname reading is Cen; the given name Shen (参, literary reading). Per S. Owen, The Great Age of Chinese Poetry: The High T’ang.

贺知章.note: He Zhizhang (659–744), Tang poet and official, Director of the Palace Library; friend of Li Bai. The novel’s Director He is modeled on him. Per Old Book of Tang, New Book of Tang.

右杀.note: A Türk title of office: princes of the Ashina royal house governing the western tribes were called the Right Shad (you sha). Here the supreme Türk commander in Chang’an, disguised as a Nestorian priest.

阿史那.note: The royal clan of the Turkic Khaganates. Standard Turkological form.

盖嘉运.note: Gai Jiayun, Tang military official who served as Protector-General of Beiting and relieved the siege of Balhuan (735). Recorded in Zizhi Tongjian.

突骑施.note: The Türgesh, a Western Turkic tribal confederation based in the Chu and Ili valleys. Standard Turkological form; see P. B. Golden, An Introduction to the History of the Turkic Peoples.

苏禄可汗.note: Suluk (Çor) Khagan (r. 716–738) of the Türgesh; besieged Balhuan in 735. Assassinated by Baga Tarkhan in 738. Standard Turkological form.

龙波.note: A Kucha craftsman and long-planted Türk agent in Chang’an, posing as a Zoroastrian believer in Huaiyuan Ward; he arranged the safe-houses and the depot and assembles the ‘Que-le Huo-duo.’ Pinyin.

王韫秀.note: Wang Zhongsi’s daughter; historically she married the minister Yuan Zai. Here a proud, foreign-fashion-loving young noblewoman. Pinyin per standard Tang sources.

葛老.note: A freed Zanj (Kunlun) slave turned the greatest slaver and underworld boss of the Pingkang Quarter; he took his surname from a former master, a vice-minister surnamed Ge. ‘Old Ge’ renders the respectful 老.

麻格儿.note: A big, insubordinate Wolf Guard, personally recruited by Cao Poyan, who defers to the Right Shad’s orders over Cao’s. Transliteration mine.

瞳儿.note: A courtesan of the First Lane in the Pingkang Quarter, Long Bo’s regular; held captive by Old Ge after eloping. Pinyin.

大萨宝.note: Head of the Sabao Office overseeing the Zoroastrian temples of the metropolitan region; a Persian resident of Chang’an of more than twenty years. 萨宝 (sabao) is an attested Tang office.

焦遂.note: One of the ‘Eight Immortals of the Wine Cup’ in Du Fu’s poem, and the only commoner among them; He Zhizhang’s old drinking friend, found murdered. Historical; pinyin.

李林甫.note: Li Linfu (d. 752), the powerful and notorious Right Chief Minister under Xuanzong; here ‘the Right Minister,’ whose mansion adjoins the Pingkang Quarter. Historical; pinyin per The Cambridge History of China, vol. 3.

李亨.note: Li Heng (711–762), Xuanzong’s heir apparent, later Emperor Suzong; the ‘one person’ behind the Jing’an Bureau. The novel’s Crown Prince. Historical; pinyin.

李白.note: Li Bai (701–762), the great Tang poet; listed among the Eight Immortals of the Wine Cup. Standard English form.

李适之.note: Li Shizhi (d. 747), Tang chief minister and one of the Eight Immortals of the Wine Cup. Pinyin.

李琎.note: Li Jin, Prince of Ruyang, a grandson of Ruizong and one of the Eight Immortals of the Wine Cup. Pinyin.

崔宗之.note: Cui Zongzhi, a Tang official and one of the Eight Immortals of the Wine Cup. Pinyin.

苏晋.note: Su Jin (676–734), a Tang official and one of the Eight Immortals of the Wine Cup. Pinyin.

张旭.note: Zhang Xu, the great ‘cursive-script sage’ of Tang calligraphy and one of the Eight Immortals of the Wine Cup. Pinyin.

小乙.note: A planted informer Zhang Xiaojing had himself placed in the underworld, now hiding in Old Ge’s den; Zhang kills him as the ‘oath-token of blood.’ Pinyin.

韩郎.note: Tong’er’s lover, an examination candidate with whom she eloped; 郎 = ‘young master.’

靳.note: The absentee Yangzhou merchant surnamed Jin who owns the derelict Xiuzheng Ward house the Türks use as a safe-house; not seen in years. Pinyin.

荀悦.note: Xun Yue (148–209), Later Han historian and thinker, author of the Shenjian (Extended Reflections), from which Li Bi quotes. Historical; standard pinyin.

李璘.note: Li Lin (d. 757), Prince Yong, a son of Emperor Xuanzong; here the polo-mad prince who backs Feng Dalun. Historically led a failed uprising along the Yangtze in 757, in which the poet Li Bai was implicated. Pinyin per The Cambridge History of China, vol. 3.

永王.note: The princely title (Prince of Yong) held by Li Lin, the emperor’s sixteenth son. Rendered ‘Prince Yong.’

元载.note: Yuan Zai (d. 777), here a lowly Evaluator of the Court of Judicial Review; historically he married Wang Yunxiu and rose to be a chief minister under Daizong, notorious for corruption, and was executed for it. Historical; pinyin.

杨慎交.note: Yang Shenjiao, husband (fuma, imperial son-in-law) of Princess Changning; famously wealthy, he built the great polo ground in Jinggong Ward. Historical; pinyin.

长宁公主.note: Princess Changning, a daughter of Emperor Zhongzong, famed for her extravagance. Historical; pinyin.

中宗.note: Emperor Zhongzong of Tang (r. 684, 705–710), uncle of the reigning Xuanzong. Standard English form.

曹王妃.en: the Consort of the Prince of Cao
曹王妃.note: The princess-consort of a Prince of Cao, to whom Prince Yong vaguely recalls Yuan Zai is connected.

贾十七.note: The head of the Changming Ward beggars, hired by Cao Poyan to keep watch; his name means ‘Seventeen.’ Pinyin.

阿罗约.note: A camel-breaker of the East Market in Zhang Xiaojing’s roll-call of ordinary Chang’an folk; the name reads as a foreign (Sogdian/Central Asian) one. Transliteration mine.

李十二.note: A dancing-girl of Chongren Ward in Zhang Xiaojing’s roll-call, who aspires to rival Lady Gongsun; her name means ‘the Twelfth.’ Pinyin.

公孙大娘.note: Lady Gongsun (fl. early 8th c.), the most celebrated sword-dancer of the Tang, whose performance Du Fu commemorated in a famous poem. Historical; standard form.

孙愐.note: Sun Mian (fl. mid-8th c.), the scholar who revised the rhyme-dictionary Tang Yun (Tang Rhymes) after 732; the watchtowers’ rhyme-code is indexed to it. Historical; pinyin.

闻无忌.note: Wen Ran’s late father, a comrade of Zhang Xiaojing’s from the Eighth Company in the Western Regions; dead the year before. Pinyin.

甘守诚.note: General of the Right Xiao Guard, who holds Zhang Xiaojing at Li Linfu’s bidding and then, cornered, wagers his release on a technicality. Pinyin.

赵参军.note: A plump, vain eighth-rank adjutant (canjun) of the Right Xiao Guard whom Tanqi cons into surrendering Zhang Xiaojing; his ranking-name 赵七郎 is rendered ‘Zhao Qilang’ (‘Seventh Son’).

董仲舒.note: Dong Zhongshu (179–104 BCE), the Han Confucian scholar who shaped the dynasty’s state ideology; his reputed tomb in Changle Ward gave the Dismount Barrow its name. Historical; standard pinyin.

贺东.note: He Zhizhang’s adopted son, a wooden man of middle years holding a minor post as vice-director in the Forestry and Crafts Bureau; praised for his pure filial devotion. Pinyin.

贺曾.note: He Zhizhang’s own son, gone off to a garrison post; named only in passing. Pinyin.

伍子胥.note: Wu Zixu (d. 484 BCE), the Chu-born statesman of Wu whose hair, legend says, turned white in a single night of anxiety as he fled through the Zhao Pass; Tanqi likens the haggard Li Bi to him. Historical/legendary; standard pinyin.

伊斯.note: The Persian deacon (zhishi) who manages the affairs of the Daqin Temple; green-eyed and sharp, he sees through Zhang Xiaojing’s disguise. The name echoes the historical priest Yisi (Yazdbōzīd) of Balkh, benefactor of the Tang Nestorian church, commemorated on the 781 Xi’an Nestorian Stele. Pinyin/standard form.

阿罗本.note: Alopen (fl. 635), the first recorded missionary of the Church of the East (Nestorian Christianity) to reach China, who came to Chang’an from Persia in 635 (Zhenguan 9) and was received by Emperor Taizong; named on the 781 Xi’an Nestorian Stele. Standard sinological form.

弥施诃.note: The Tang Nestorian transliteration of the Messiah (Syriac məšĪḥā), that is Jesus Christ; the form appears in the surviving Tang Nestorian scriptures. Rendered by transliteration, as the source has it.

庞录事.note: A long-faced registrar (lushi) of the Jing’an Bureau, secretly in the pay of the Secretariat (the Right Minister’s men); he passes intelligence out through the corner gate and is caught by Xu Bin. Pinyin.

普遮.note: The name under which the Right Shad hides at the Daqin Temple: a Sogdian elder said to hold an ordination certificate from the Nestorian temple of Kang, arrived a month before. Found stabbed in this chapter; his old modao scar and armor-calluses betray him as a career cavalryman, that is the Right Shad. Transliteration mine.

吉温.note: Ji Wen (d. 755), a Tang official notorious as a hatchet-man and torturer of confessions, client of Li Linfu and later of An Lushan; here appointed to take over the Jing’an Bureau for the Secretariat. Historical; pinyin. Footnoted at first appearance.

来俊臣.note: Lai Junchen (d. 697), the archetypal ‘cruel official’ under Wu Zetian, a torturer and framer of cases whose very name terrifies; author of the Luozhi jing. Historical; pinyin. Footnoted at first appearance.

周兴.note: Zhou Xing (d. 691), a cruel official of Wu Zetian’s reign, remembered with Lai Junchen (the idiom ‘please, step into the jar’ is his); the torture ‘the flying stone that summons the immortal’ is laid to him. Historical; pinyin.

周利贞.note: Zhou Lizhen (fl. early 8th c.), a cruel official of the Shenlong era who, at Wu Sansi’s order, tortured Huan Yanfan to death; the killing named ‘sunset-glow on the bamboo.’ Historical; pinyin.

桓彦范.note: Huan Yanfan (653–706), a Tang statesman, one of the five who forced Wu Zetian’s abdication in the 705 Shenlong coup; later hounded to a savage death by Wu Sansi’s man Zhou Lizhen. Historical; pinyin.

武三思.note: Wu Sansi (d. 707), nephew of Empress Wu Zetian, a powerful and unscrupulous prince of the Wu clan who took vengeance on the Shenlong restorers. Historical; pinyin.

郝象贤.note: Hao Xiangxian (d. 687), a Tang official executed under Wu Zetian on Zhou Xing’s fabricated charge; the torture ‘the flying stone that summons the immortal’ is told of his case. Historical; pinyin.

公辅.note: Yuan Zai’s courtesy name (zi), by which Ji Wen addresses him as they stage-manage the takeover of the Jing’an Bureau.

刘十七.note: A Shouzhuolang assassin, one of the two planted in the Persian Temple; his name means ‘Seventeen.’ He gives Zhang Xiaojing the passwords to the firepoint before dying, and is killed in his escort-cart in this chapter. Pinyin.

摩伽罗.note: The code-name of another Shouzhuolang, paired with Liu Shiqi as one the firepoint expects; a transliteration of Sanskrit Makara (the sea-monster, cf. 摩羯 = makara). Kept as the pinyin transliteration to distinguish the person from the decorative motif.

鱼肠.note: The one-armed assassin who cuts every thread for the Türk conspiracy, killing the firemaster and Liu Shiqi; he names himself after the ancient dagger Yuchang (‘fish-gut’). Kept as the pinyin of the weapon-name. Footnoted at first appearance.

卑路斯.note: Peroz III (fl. 7th c.), son of Yazdegerd III, last of the Sasanian royal line of Persia; fled to the Tang court after the Arab conquest and was given an honorary generalship. Yisi claims descent from his exiled house. Standard sinological form. Footnoted at first appearance.

太宗.note: Emperor Taizong of Tang (r. 626–649), the dynasty’s second and most celebrated ruler. Standard English form.

高宗.note: Emperor Gaozong of Tang (r. 649–683), son of Taizong; under him the Persian refugees reached Chang’an. Standard English form.

管仲.note: Guan Zhong (d. 645 BCE), the great minister who made Duke Huan of Qi the first hegemon of the Spring and Autumn period; traditionally honored as the patron of the courtesan trade. Historical; standard pinyin. Footnoted at first appearance.

老聃.note: Lao Dan, that is Laozi, the reputed author of the Daodejing; Yuan Zai quotes its 36th chapter. Rendered by the personal name the source uses.

燕子李.note: A notorious thief once hunted by the ward watch, recalled by the old post-soldier Old Zhao as the occasion Zhang Xiaojing saved his life. 燕子 (‘swallow’) is the roof-running burglar’s byname.

老赵.note: An aging post-soldier of the Pingkang Ward watch who once served under Zhang Xiaojing and helps him slip the cordon; distinct from Adjutant Zhao (赵参军). 老 renders the familiar ‘Old.’

张洛.note: A recorder of the Forestry and Crafts Bureau, saddled with the thankless charge of the great lantern-tower. Pinyin.

韦氏.note: The heir apparent Li Heng’s principal wife, styled here 太子妃 (consort of the heir). Rendered ‘Consort Wei.’

太真.note: The Daoist name of Yang Yuhuan (719–756), later Yang Guifei. Pinyin follows the standard scholarly form.

晁分.note: A master craftsman of Chang’an, a native of Izumo in Japan and servant of Chao Heng; he built the sand-table of Chang’an for the Jing’an Bureau, reads the bamboo offcuts, and gives Zhang Xiaojing the knife, crossbow, and the secret way into the lantern-tower. Pinyin of the Chinese surname 晁.

晁衡.note: Chao Heng, the Chinese name of Abe no Nakamaro (698–770), the Japanese student-envoy who became a high Tang official; here Chao Fen’s master-house, styled Vice-Minister of the Court of the Imperial Regalia. Historical; footnoted at first appearance.

毛顺.note: Mao Shun, the master lantern-maker, styled Director of Lanterns, designer of the Taishang Xuanyuan Grand Lantern-Tower; coerced by Long Bo through a threat to his family. A craftsman of this name is recorded in Tang sources as having built a great lantern-tower for the court. Pinyin.

毛婆罗.note: Mao Shun’s father, a painter and carver who served as Aide in the Directorate for Imperial Manufactories under the Wu Zhou and cast the Tianshu column before the Duanmen Gate. Pinyin (the name 婆罗 reads as a foreign one).

许合子.note: Xu Hezi (also written 许和子), byname Yongxin, the most famous woman singer of Xuanzong’s court; here a lantern-float star whose cart Zhang Xiaojing commandeers. Historical; footnoted at first appearance. Pinyin.

杨玉环.note: Yang Yuhuan (719–756), later Yang Guifei; the same person as Taizhen (太真), the Daoist name under which she waits at Xuanzong’s side. Originally the consort of Prince Shou. Pinyin per standard scholarship.

寿王.note: The princely title (Prince of Shou) held by Li Mao, a son of Emperor Xuanzong and Yang Yuhuan’s first husband. Rendered ‘Prince Shou.’

李瑁.note: Li Mao (d. 775), Prince Shou, a son of Emperor Xuanzong; Yang Yuhuan was taken from him into the palace. Historical; pinyin.

窦太后.note: The Zhaocheng Empress Dowager, née Dou, Xuanzong’s mother; praying for her blessing was the pretext under which Yang Yuhuan was made a Daoist nun. Historical.

萧规.note: The true name of Long Bo (see 龙波): once an archer of the Eighth Company at the beacon-fort, comrade of Zhang Xiaojing and Wen Wuji. After a corrupt county-aide destroyed his family he turned outlaw, and became the mastermind who plans the destruction of the lantern-tower under the alias Long Bo. Pinyin.

赵孝.note: One of a pair of Later Han brothers (with 赵礼 Zhao Li) proverbial for fraternal love, each offering himself to bandits to spare the other; a lantern-figure in the ‘Tangdi’ chamber. Recorded in the Hou Han shu.

赵礼.note: Brother of Zhao Xiao (see 赵孝); a lantern-figure in the ‘Tangdi’ chamber of brotherly love.

李卫公.note: Li Jing (571–649), enfeoffed Duke of Wei, the foremost general of the early Tang; his 630 campaign that crushed the Eastern Türks in the Yin Mountains is the subject of a lantern-chamber. Title plus pinyin.

孔圣.note: Confucius (551–479 BCE), ‘the Sage’ 孔圣; shown in a lantern-chamber questioning Laozi, to figure the way of civil governance.

老子.note: The sage Laozi, = Lao Dan (see 老聃); honored 太上玄元 by the Tang house. Pinyin.

陈玄礼.note: Historical general (d. after 762); commander of the palace guard under Xuanzong, later famous as the man who at the Mawei post-station in 756 forced the deaths of Yang Guozhong and Yang Guifei during the flight from An Lushan’s rebellion. Here Grand General of the Longwu Army. Pinyin.

安禄山.note: Historical general (c. 703–757) of Sogdian and Turkic parentage; in 744 the military commissioner of Pinglu, later of Fanyang and Hedong as well. In 755 he raised the rebellion that shattered the High Tang, taking Chang’an and forcing Xuanzong’s flight; killed by his own son in 757. Pinyin.

颉利可汗.note: Illig Qaghan (r. 620–630), last ruler of the Eastern Turkic Khaganate, captured in 630 by the Tang general Li Jing (Duke Li of Wei) in the Yin Mountains campaign; the tableau of the lantern-chamber. Pinyin follows the conventional scholarly rendering of the Chinese form.

李隆基.note: Personal name of Emperor Xuanzong (685–762), the reigning Son of Heaven of the novel. Pinyin follows the standard scholarly form.

韦后.note: Empress Wei (d. 710), consort of Emperor Zhongzong, who is said to have poisoned him and seized power; overthrown and killed in the Tanglong coup of 710. Distinct from 韦氏, the heir apparent’s Consort Wei of the present reign.

太平公主.note: Princess Taiping (d. 713), daughter of Emperor Gaozong and Empress Wu; ally of Li Longji in the Tanglong coup, then destroyed by him in the Xiantian coup of 713.

吉顼.note: Ji Xu (d. 700), Tang chancellor under Empress Wu; here named as the uncle (whose brother’s-son he was) of Ji Wen. Historical; pinyin.

薛嶷.note: Litterateur to the heir apparent (太子文学), who recommended Ji Wen to the throne only for the Son of Heaven to reject him. Pinyin.

登徒子.note: Tanqi’s teasing nickname for Zhang Xiaojing, from the byword 登徒子 (‘Master Dengtu,’ the lecher of Song Yu’s rhapsody). Rendered by sense as ‘lecher’ throughout (dominant rendering ch02-ch13).

郭氏.note: Prince Yong (Li Lin)’s mother, who prayed at the Guanyin temple in Jinggong Ward during his childhood illness and died soon after; her spirit-tablet stands there. ch20.

伍归一.note: A Pifu, a man of Hejian falsely charged with desertion; named by Xiao Gui before the Son of Heaven. ch20.

莫洼儿.note: A Pifu, a Hu of mixed blood from Jincheng, ruined by an imperial camel-levy. ch20.

索法惠.note: A Pifu, a cartwright of Henan County ruined by lantern-fair corvée; he burns the fleeing envoy alive. ch20.

甘校尉.note: Commandant of the Eighth Company, who taught them in the Western Regions (‘forethought brings success’); among the dead whose ashes were brought back. First named ch15, recurs ch20.

刘文办.note: An Eighth Company comrade among the dead of the Western Regions. First named ch15, recurs in the death-roll ch20.

宋十六.note: An Eighth Company comrade among the dead; the 十六 (‘Sixteen’) is a ranking-name. First named ch15, recurs ch20.

杜婆罗.note: An Eighth Company comrade among the dead. First named ch15, recurs ch20.

王河东.note: An Eighth Company comrade, a Hedong man (as ‘Old Wang…Hedong’ ch15; in the death-roll as 王河东 ch20).

樊老四.note: An Eighth Company comrade (Old Fan, of Jiannan). First ch15; in the death-roll as 樊老四 ch20.

曹刿.note: The commoner strategist of Lu in the Zuozhuan (曹刿论战); Xiao Gui quotes his ‘those who eat meat are of mean discernment.’ ch20 (see note).

隋炀帝.note: Yang Guang (569–618), last effective emperor of the Sui, a byword for a ruler brought down by extravagance and misrule. ch20.

轧荦山.note: A Persian war-god idol hidden atop the Qinzheng Wuben Tower; the name was also the childhood name of the rebel general An Lushan (安禄山). See the note at its first appearance (ch21).

贞顺武皇后.note: Consort Wu Huifei (武惠妃, d. 737), Xuanzong’s most beloved consort, posthumously raised to empress with the name Zhenshun. Mother of Li Mao (Prince Shou) and of the plot to depose the heir apparent Li Ying.

武惠妃.note: The living style of the woman posthumously titled Empress Wu Zhenshun; Huifei is her consort rank.

李瑛.note: Xuanzong’s eldest surviving son and heir apparent until 737, framed by Consort Wu and driven to his death; the title then passed to Li Heng.

高祖.note: Li Yuan (566–635), founding emperor of the Tang. Rendered by temple name, as with Taizong/Gaozong already in the glossary.

赫连勃勃.note: Xiongnu founder (r. 407–425) of the Xia kingdom of the Sixteen Kingdoms period; builder of the fortress-capital Tongwan, cited here for the legendary hardness of its rammed-earth walls. Pinyin. (Noted at ch22.)

陆三.note: The main-hall runner of the Jing’an Bureau and the traitor within; surnamed Lu (陆), third-born (行三), a man of Yuezhou, once a soldier, secretly an agent of the Shouzhuolang planted by the Pinglu resident-agent courtyard. ‘San’ renders 行三, ‘the third.’ ch23.

刘骆谷.note: The manager of the Pinglu resident-agent courtyard in the capital and a confidant of An Lushan’s; thick-browed and soldierly, but smooth as a merchant. He gives Li Bi the master-ledger that traces the plot’s paymaster to the Shengping physic garden. Pinyin. ch24.

张守珪.note: Zhang Shougui (684–740), Tang military commissioner of Youzhou/Pinglu on the northeastern frontier; the historical general who took the young An Lushan as his adopted son. Named only in passing. Historical; pinyin.

白眉可汗.note: The Türk khagan who briefly succeeded Ozmish and was killed the next year (745); the Second Turkic Khaganate then collapsed and its remnant was absorbed by the Uyghurs. 白眉 = ‘White Brows.’ Romanization provisional.

杨国忠.note: A cousin of Yang Guifei who rose to be chief minister of the late Tianbao court; put to death by the mutinous guards at Mawei in 756. Standard pinyin.

韦坚.note: A Tang official and affine of the heir apparent; his case (韦坚案, 746) was one of Li Linfu’s purges of the crown prince’s circle.

杜有邻.note: Father-in-law of the heir apparent; the Du Youlin case (747) was another of Li Linfu’s prosecutions that struck at the crown prince’s intimates.

郭子仪.note: The great Tang general (697–781) whose campaigns were decisive in suppressing the An Lushan Rebellion; ennobled Prince of Fenyang. Standard form.

李辅国.note: The powerful eunuch who dominated the courts of Suzong and Daizong. Standard pinyin.

玄宗.note: Temple name of Emperor Li Longji (r. 712–756), the reigning ‘Son of Heaven’ / ‘the Sage’ of the novel; the name-form appears in the afterword’s historical epilogue.

肃宗.note: Temple name of Li Heng (r. 756–762), the heir apparent of the novel, who took the throne at Lingwu during the rebellion.

代宗.note: Temple name of the emperor (r. 762–779) who followed Suzong; recalled Li Bi to the chancellorship and later had Yuan Zai executed.

德宗.note: Temple name of the emperor (r. 779–805) who followed Daizong; the last of the four sovereigns Li Bi served.

杨贵妃.note: The Precious Consort Yang, the same person as Taizhen (太真) of the novel; strangled at Mawei in 756. Standard form.

于赓哲.note: A modern historian of the Tang, thanked by the author in Afterword II. Pinyin.

惊鸿.note: One of the friends thanked in Afterword II; an online handle, romanized in pinyin (lit. ‘startled swan’).

扫书喵.note: One of the friends thanked in Afterword II; an online handle, romanized in pinyin (lit. ‘book-sweeping cat’).

森林鹿.note: One of the friends thanked in Afterword II; an online handle, romanized in pinyin (lit. ‘forest deer’).

黑肚皮小蹄.note: One of the friends thanked in Afterword II; an online handle, romanized in pinyin (lit. ‘black-belly little-hoof’).

靖安司.note: A newly created security office charged with threat-prevention (zei shi ce fang) for the whole western capital. The name is glossed in the text: ‘to quell revolt is jing; when the four quarters are without trouble, that is an.’ Si = bureau.

旅贲军.note: An elite guard unit under the Jing’an Bureau, here commanded by Cui Qi. The name derives from an ancient palace-guard title; no settled English form exists.

金吾卫.note: The Gold Bird Guard, responsible for patrolling the streets of the capital and enforcing the night curfew.

京兆府.note: The metropolitan prefecture governing Chang’an and its two counties.

萨宝府.note: The Tang office administering resident foreign (chiefly Sogdian) communities and their Zoroastrian temples, headed by the sabao.

将作监.en: the Directorate for the Palace Buildings
将作监.note: The Tang directorate in charge of state construction and public works; the Wolf Guards impersonate its road-repair laborers. Rendering per C. O. Hucker.

苏记车马行.note: A reputable haulage firm working the routes north of Chang’an; it unwittingly carries the Türks’ cargo from Yanzhou.

宣徽院.note: A Tang palace agency overseeing court provisioning and ceremonial; the Five Kennels (五坊) fall under it. Rendering per C. O. Hucker, A Dictionary of Official Titles in Imperial China.

尚池署.note: The office that manages Qujiang Pool, independent of the wards and their street-posts, so the Nine-Gate Drum has no authority over it.

工部.note: One of the Six Ministries, in charge of state construction and public works; Feng Dalun holds a lowly post in it. Rendering per C. O. Hucker.

虞部.note: A bureau (the Yu Section) under the Ministry of Works, overseeing the capital’s repairs, dredging, and upkeep; the fat post Feng Dalun exploits. Rendering per C. O. Hucker.

大理寺.note: The central Tang court of justice, which reviewed serious criminal cases. Rendering per C. O. Hucker.

御史台.note: The Tang organ of surveillance and impeachment, whose censors could denounce officials on hearsay. Rendering per C. O. Hucker.

刑部.note: One of the Six Ministries, in charge of law and punishments. Rendering per C. O. Hucker.

内侍省.note: The eunuch-staffed agency of the inner palace, to which the Five Kennels and their keepers answered. Rendering per C. O. Hucker.

右骁卫.note: One of the Tang Sixteen Guards of the Southern Command; its elite Leopard Cavalry are first to muster at the death-line. Rendering per C. O. Hucker.

豹骑.note: The elite mounted troops of the Right Xiao Guard. Rendered literally.

南衙十六卫.en: the Sixteen Guards of the Southern Command
南衙十六卫.note: The Tang metropolitan guard system (the ‘southern’ offices, as against the ‘northern’ palace armies) of sixteen guard commands headquartered in the imperial city. Rendering per C. O. Hucker.

仓曹.note: The section (cangcao) of a Tang guard command in charge of stores and provisions, here also of changing the daily door-registers. Rendered ‘the Stores Section.’

中书省.note: One of the three great departments of the Tang central government, which drafted imperial edicts; the Right Minister Li Linfu’s power base. Rendering per C. O. Hucker.

凤阁.note: An archaic byname for the Secretariat (中书省), from its Wu-Zhou-era renaming; Registrar Pang uses it for the office he secretly serves. Rendered literally, ‘the Phoenix Pavilion.’

祠部.note: The bureau under the Ministry of Rites overseeing state religious affairs and the registers of Buddhist, Daoist, and foreign clergy; it keeps the roll of Nestorian temples. Rendering per C. O. Hucker.

守捉郎.note: A guild of mercenaries recruited out of the frontier garrison-towns (守捉), hiring themselves to officials, military commissioners, and merchants; two of its assassins are planted in the Persian Temple. The novel’s extrapolation from a real Tang institution (see the term 守捉城). Kept as the transliteration ‘the Shouzhuolang’; a member is a Shouzhuolang. Footnoted at first appearance.

右威卫.note: One of the Tang Sixteen Guards of the Southern Command; the guard in which the refugee Persian prince Peroz was given an honorary generalship. Rendering per C. O. Hucker.

龙武军.note: The Militant Dragon Army, one of the Tang northern (palace) armies most trusted by the emperor; here charged with the outer cordon of the Xingqing Palace. Rendered ‘the Longwu Army’ (pinyin), as with the Jinwu Guard.

兵部.note: One of the Six Ministries; here it runs the selection of foot-archers that gives Zhang Xiaojing his Chang’an post. Rendering per Hucker.

折冲府.note: The local headquarters of the Tang fubing militia system; some of Xiao Gui’s veterans come from these. Rendering per Hucker.

左骁卫.note: The left wing of the Xiao Guards of the Sixteen Guards, paired with the Right Xiao Guard (右骁卫) already glossed. Same rendering, ‘Left’ for 左.

千牛卫.note: One of the Sixteen Guards, the imperial bodyguard whose officers bore the ‘thousand-ox’ sword; kept in pinyin (the numeral 千 is part of the unit’s name, not a count).

万骑.note: The ‘Ten-Thousand Horse,’ an elite guard cavalry of Wu Zetian’s and Zhongzong’s reigns, a forerunner of the Longwu Army; kept in pinyin (the 万 is part of the name, not a count).

羽林军.note: The Feather-Forest Army, a household guard of the Northern Command; one of the night-watch guards attending the Son of Heaven. Kept in pinyin like the Longwu Army.

监门卫.note: The Palace Gate Guard among the Sixteen Guards, charged with warding the palace gates; rendered by function.

户部.note: One of the Six Ministries, charged with population, land and revenue (Hucker: Ministry of Revenue); Xu Bin was seconded from it to the Jing’an Bureau. ch20.

西域都护府.en: the Protectorate of the Western Regions
西域都护府.note: The frontier protectorate-general under which the Eighth Company served (cf. the Protectorate of Anxi, 安西都护府). ch20.

南衙.note: The Southern Command: the metropolitan guard forces under the civil government (their offices lying south of the palace), as opposed to the Northern Command’s palace guards. Hucker-style rendering.

北衙.note: The Northern Command: the emperor’s own palace guard armies (Longwu, Yulin, and the rest, quartered north of the palace), as opposed to the Southern Command. Hucker-style rendering.

大理司.note: A source variant for 大理寺 (the Court of Judicial Review), the high court; Yuan Zai is its 评事 (Evaluator). Rendered with the decided form for 大理寺.

长安.note: The Tang capital, on the site of modern Xi’an; the greatest city in the world of its day. Standard English form.

长安县.note: The western of the two counties into which the capital was divided, west of the Vermilion Bird Avenue.

万年县.note: The eastern county of the capital, home to many of the great and noble houses.

西市.note: One of Chang’an’s two great licensed markets, thronged with foreign merchants.

东市.note: The eastern of the capital’s two licensed markets.

光德坊.note: The residential ward east of the West Market where the Jing’an Bureau sits. Fang = ward, a walled residential block.

朱雀大街.note: Chang’an’s central north–south avenue (Zhuque, the Vermilion Bird of the south), dividing the city into its two counties. Also called the Vermilion Bird Way.

广通渠.note: A canal running past the West Market, widened for timber barges; Cao Poyan escapes down it.

独柳树.note: The West Market’s execution ground, shunned as unlucky.

康国.note: The Sogdian city-state of Samarkand, one of the ‘Nine Surnames of Zhaowu.’ Standard sinological identification.

拂林.note: The Tang name for Byzantium / the Eastern Roman lands. Standard identification.

怀远坊.note: A ward south of the West Market, home to a large foreign population and a Zoroastrian temple.

安仁坊.note: A ward northeast of Dunyi Ward where the Wang military commissioner’s family resides.

安业坊.note: A ward containing the Jidu Nunnery, whose purple-gold bell is Wen Ran’s landmark.

崇业坊.note: A ward where the Xuandu Abbey causes heavy traffic jams.

怀贞坊.note: A ward across the street from Chongye Ward where Feng Dalun watches from a wine-house.

敦义坊.note: A ward south of the West Market where Wen Ran’s incense shop is located.

拨换城.note: A garrison town of the Protectorate of Anxi, near modern Aksu in Xinjiang. Site of the 735 siege described in Li Bi’s backstory for Zhang Xiaojing.

小勃律.note: A kingdom in the high Karakoram (modern Gilgit-Baltistan); Tanqi’s mother was from there. Standard identification per Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia.

玄都观.note: A major Daoist temple in Chongye Ward, frequented by the great and powerful.

积度尼寺.note: A Buddhist nunnery in Anye Ward where Empress Wu Zetian once took the veil; famous for its purple-gold bell.

大秦.note: The Tang name for the Eastern Roman / Byzantine lands or sometimes the Near East in general. Standard identification.

大食.note: The Tang name for the Arab/Umayyad (later Abbasid) caliphate. Standard identification.

龟兹.note: The great Buddhist oasis kingdom on the northern Silk Road (modern Kuqa, Xinjiang); Long Bo’s origin. Standard identification.

平康里.note: Chang’an’s entertainment district in the northeast of the city. 平康坊, the administrative ward, is rendered ‘Pingkang Ward’; 平康里, the pleasure quarter within it, ‘the Pingkang Quarter.’

延州.note: A prefecture north of Chang’an (modern Yan’an, Shaanxi), whence the Türks’ cargo is hauled. Standard.

修政坊.note: A ward in the southern city; Long Bo’s safe-house lies southwest of its crossroads.

太平坊.note: A ward west of the Vermilion Bird Avenue, facing the imperial city’s Hanguang Gate; site of the Shiji Temple where Li Bi meets the Crown Prince.

含光门.note: A southern gate of the imperial city of Chang’an.

实际寺.note: A Buddhist temple in Taiping Ward, housing the ‘finest in the capital’ Pure Land Cloister.

净土院.note: A famous cloister within the Shiji Temple, its bamboo grove holding a hundred and eight clay Buddhas.

荐福寺.note: A great temple in Anren Ward whose golden pagoda-spire is a landmark from the Vermilion Bird Avenue (the historical Small Wild Goose Pagoda stands in its grounds).

延寿坊.note: A ward near the North Yong’an Canal where Jiao Sui’s body is found.

永安渠.note: A canal of Chang’an; its northern reach (永安北渠, the North Yong’an Canal) runs by Yanshou Ward, where Cao Poyan is thought to have come ashore.

殖业坊.note: A ward west of the Vermilion Bird Avenue.

丰乐坊.note: A ward west of the Vermilion Bird Avenue, near Zhiye Ward.

光福坊.note: A ward on the route south from Anren Ward.

靖善坊.note: A ward in the southern city; past it the streets grow sparse and desolate.

曲江池.note: The great scenic lake-and-garden district in the southeast corner of Chang’an, half within the walls and half without; a famous Tang pleasure-ground. Standard identification.

芙蓉苑.note: The imperial pleasure-park (the Lotus Garden) adjoining Qujiang Pool. Standard identification.

少陵原.note: The loess tableland southeast of Chang’an, abutting the outer half of Qujiang Pool; Du Fu styled himself ‘the Old Man of Shaoling’ after it. Standard.

启夏门.note: The eastern of the two gates in the south wall of Chang’an’s outer city, close to Qujiang Pool. Standard.

延兴门.note: The southern of the gates in the east wall of Chang’an, close to Qujiang Pool. Standard.

筑心阁.note: A two-story viewing-pavilion (its name 筑心, ‘building the heart’) in the Türks’ Xiuzheng Ward safe-house, rigged with castor oil; it burns down in this chapter.

岭南.note: The far south of Tang China, below the Nanling ranges (roughly modern Guangdong and Guangxi); source of the snake-vine rope. Standard.

陇山.note: The range on the Shaanxi–Gansu border marking the old northwest frontier; Cui Qi’s origin as a frontier soldier. Standard.

大宁坊.note: A ward on the fourth street east of the Vermilion Bird Avenue, close to the Daming and Xingqing Palaces; home to many officials, and to Feng Dalun’s residence.

靖恭坊.note: A ward at the easternmost edge of Chang’an, against the city wall; site of the great polo ground where Prince Yong plays.

通济坊.note: A ward at the south end of the eastern city; site of the palace Dog Kennel from which Zhang Xiaojing seizes a hound.

光行坊.note: A ward in the southwest of Chang’an; the northeast corner of the crossroads called Guangxing-Anle, where the hound loses the scent.

安乐坊.note: A ward in the southwest of Chang’an; the southwest corner of the crossroads called Guangxing-Anle.

亲仁坊.note: A ward named alongside Anren as an example of the most lavish noble residences, unlike the plainer houses of Daning Ward.

大明宫.note: The great palace complex in the northeast of Chang’an, the chief seat of the Tang court. Standard identification.

兴庆宫.note: A palace in the eastern part of Chang’an, favored residence of Emperor Xuanzong. Standard identification.

延喜门.note: A gate of the imperial city, bordering Daning Ward on the west.

斡难河.note: A river of the northeastern steppe (in modern Mongolia and Siberia), where Cao Poyan’s daughter gathered the pebbles of her necklace. Standard geographic form (the Onon, later the heartland of the rising Mongols).

鄂尔浑河.note: The central river of the Mongolian steppe, historic seat of the Turkic and later Uyghur khaganates; Wang Zhongsi’s campaigns reach its banks. Standard geographic form.

河东.note: The region east of the Yellow River’s great bend (roughly modern Shanxi); here the breed-origin of Zhang Xiaojing’s borrowed sighthound. Standard.

慈恩寺.note: A great Buddhist temple of Chang’an (site of the Great Wild Goose Pagoda); cited proverbially for its monks’ strict vegetarian rule. Standard identification.

油洒地.note: The name of the polo ground in Jinggong Ward built by Yang Shenjiao: the earth was sprinkled with oil to lay the dust. Rendered literally.

金光门.note: The middle of the three gates in the west wall of Chang’an, one street west of the West Market; the road every westbound caravan used. Standard.

昌明坊.note: A large, desolate ward in the southwest of Chang’an under Chang’an County; the Türks hide their depot in a disused brick-and-tile kiln here.

日南王宅.note: A great derelict mansion in the southeast corner of Changming Ward, built in the Zhenguan years by a visiting King of Rinan (日南, a Tang commandery in what is now central Vietnam) and long abandoned; Cao Poyan names it as a decoy hiding-place.

大雁塔.note: The Great Wild Goose Pagoda, the famous brick pagoda in the grounds of the Ci’en Temple in Chang’an. Standard identification.

升道坊.note: A ward in Zhang Xiaojing’s roll-call of ordinary Chang’an, home to an old Uyghur bilo-cake maker.

普济寺.note: A temple in Zhang Xiaojing’s roll-call, famed for its wild-rice served on the first and fifteenth of the month.

安邑坊.note: A ward in Zhang Xiaojing’s roll-call, where the camel-breaker Aluoyue dreams of settling.

长兴坊.note: A ward in Zhang Xiaojing’s roll-call, home to a Court Music flute-player surnamed Xue.

天津桥.note: A famous bridge over the Luo River at Luoyang; here the spot where the flute-player of Zhang’s roll-call plays at midnight. (The novel places the recollection in the capital region generally.) Standard identification.

崇仁坊.note: A ward in Zhang Xiaojing’s roll-call, home to the dancing-girl Li Shi’er.

龙首渠.note: One of the canals feeding Chang’an, drawn from the Chan River; here the water along which a blind old woman hawks paper boats. Standard.

永安坊.note: A ward west of the Vermilion Bird Avenue; the northeast corner of the crossroads called Yong’an-Tonggui, where the Türks turn north.

通规坊.note: A ward west of the Vermilion Bird Avenue; the southwest corner of the crossroads called Yong’an-Tonggui.

归义坊.note: A ward paired with Dunyi Ward at the crossroads called Dunyi-Guiyi (East Dunyi / West Guiyi), where the chase first stalls.

延福坊.note: A ward at the crossroads called Yanfu-Yongping, on the northward chase.

永平坊.note: A ward at the crossroads called Yanfu-Yongping, on the northward chase.

崇贤坊.note: A ward on the third street; a watchtower reports carts ‘south of Chongxian Ward.’

长寿坊.note: A ward on the fourth street west of the Vermilion Bird Gate Avenue; part of the crossroads called Changshou-Daixian.

待贤坊.note: A ward on the fourth street west of the Vermilion Bird Gate Avenue; part of the crossroads called Changshou-Daixian.

居德坊.note: A ward along which the Guangtong Canal flows into the West Market.

群贤坊.note: A ward along which the Guangtong Canal flows into the West Market.

秦岭.note: The great mountain range south of Chang’an, source of the timber floated down the Guangtong Canal. Standard.

庐陵.note: A prefecture in what is now Jiangxi (modern Ji’an); the native place of the flute-player Xue in Zhang’s roll-call. Standard.

洛阳.note: The Tang eastern capital; a small band of musicians hired for a noble’s birthday comes from there. Standard English form.

酒泉.note: A prefecture of the Hexi corridor (modern Gansu), named with Yumen and Yanzhou as a source of rock-oil. Standard.

玉门.note: A frontier town of the Hexi corridor (modern Gansu), named as a source of rock-oil. Standard.

移香阁.note: Feng Dalun’s small luxury pavilion, its plaster kneaded with Khotan fragrant grass so that shifting sunlight releases a perfume; the name 移香 means ‘the shifting fragrance.’

常乐坊.note: An eastern ward of Chang’an, site of the Toad Barrow and famed for its Langguan Clear wine.

虾蟆陵.note: A vinegrowing mound in Changle Ward famed for its wine. Its true name was the Dismount Barrow (下马陵, Xiama Ling), from the ancient tomb where Confucians dismounted in respect; the vulgar corrupted 下马 (xiama) into the homophonous 虾蟆 (hama, ‘toad’). Rendered by sense in both forms.

于阗.note: The great Buddhist oasis kingdom of the southern Silk Road (modern Hotan, Xinjiang); source of the fragrant grass in the Yixiang Pavilion’s walls. Standard identification.

宣平坊.note: A ward on the northeast of the Leyou Plateau in Wannian County, where He Zhizhang keeps his willow-shaded house.

乐游原.note: The loess height in the southeast of Chang’an, a famous scenic resort (paired with Qujiang Pool as ‘the hills and waters’); so thick with willows it was nicknamed ‘the Willow Capital.’ Standard identification.

新昌坊.note: One of the four wards on the Leyou Plateau.

升平坊.note: A ward on the Leyou Plateau, south of Xuanping; site of an Eastern Palace physic-garden that supplies He Zhizhang’s medicines.

青龙寺.note: A great temple on the Leyou Plateau, later famous as a center of Tang esoteric Buddhism. Standard identification.

崇真观.note: A large Daoist abbey (guan) on the Leyou Plateau.

慈悲寺.note: A charitable temple in Guangde Ward, a single wall from the Jing’an Bureau (Sun Simiao’s old residence); the text derives its name 慈悲 (‘Compassion’) from the Sui-era almsgiving of a monk named Tanxian. Li Bi installs Zhang Xiaojing in a hut in its grounds.

常法寺.note: One of the temples set about the corners of Guangde Ward.

胜光寺.note: One of the temples set about the corners of Guangde Ward.

承天门.note: The great south gate of the palace-city of Chang’an, opening onto the imperial city; the Right Xiao Guard offices stand between it and the Zhuque Gate. Standard identification.

朱雀门.note: The central south gate of the imperial city (the Vermilion Bird Gate), at the head of the Vermilion Bird Avenue.

义宁坊.note: A ward at the far northwest corner of Chang’an, beside the Kaiyuan Gate; site of the city’s oldest Nestorian temple, the mother-temple of the faith in China.

开远门.note: The northernmost of the three gates in the west wall of Chang’an. Standard.

布政坊.note: A ward near Yining Ward that also holds a Nestorian temple; parties are sent to search it.

延康坊.note: A ward near Yining Ward that also holds a Nestorian temple; parties are sent to search it.

大秦寺.note: The Nestorian temple of Yining Ward. Officially styled the Persian Temple (波斯寺) until Emperor Xuanzong’s 745 (Tianbao 4) decree renamed all such temples 大秦寺 after the faith’s true origin in Daqin (the Roman Orient); Yisi’s insistence on the name here anticipates that change by a year. Standard identification.

波斯寺.note: The official Tang name for a Nestorian temple before the 745 renaming; see the Daqin Temple. Rendered literally.

嘉会坊.note: A ward not far south of the Jing’an Bureau where the main force of the Lüben Guards is quartered; Li Bi counts on relief coming from it.

仙州.note: The prefecture (modern Nanyang, Henan) in which the poet Cen Shen’s family was registered; he names himself ‘Cen Shen of Xianzhou.’ The source writes 远怀坊 for 怀远坊 (Huaiyuan Ward) as the scene of his earlier interference; rendered by the intended referent. Standard.

刘记书肆.note: A bookshop inside Pingkang Ward where the Shouzhuolang take delivery of their lodgings and their commissions. Rendered by sense.

兴道坊.note: A ward east of the Vermilion Bird Avenue; the first watchtower to answer Zhang Xiaojing’s purple-lantern signal.

开化坊.note: A ward south of Xingdao Ward whose watchtower relays Zhang Xiaojing’s lantern-signal.

光禄坊.note: A ward west of the Vermilion Bird Avenue, at the edge of the crowd waiting to see the lantern-floats.

务本坊.note: A ward whose watchtower wakes in turn to Zhang Xiaojing’s lantern-signal.

崇义坊.note: A ward whose watchtower wakes in turn to Zhang Xiaojing’s lantern-signal.

勤政务本楼.note: The ‘Tower of Diligent Governance and Attending to the Root,’ a gate-tower of the Xingqing Palace from which Emperor Xuanzong appeared before the people; here the winning lantern-float performer is to light the great lantern-tower beside the Son of Heaven. Historical building; rendered by its name.

楼兰.note: The ancient kingdom of Kroraina/Loulan on the Lop Nor route, long a byword for the desolate far frontier; in Cen Shen’s poem, ‘the garrison boys of Loulan.’ Standard identification.

秦山.note: The mountains of the Qin region about Chang’an, in Cen Shen’s poem paired against the clouds of the Long Mountains. Rendered by sense.

岐山.note: Mount Qi and the district around it, west of Chang’an in Fufeng (modern Shaanxi), an ancient Zhou heartland; the country home of the Muhu song Tanqi hums. Standard.

烽燧城.note: The frontier beacon-fort in the Western Regions whose desperate defense Zhang Xiaojing and Wen Wuji survived (three of the garrison lived); the root of their friendship and of Zhang’s backstory. Rendered ‘the beacon-fort.’

雍州.note: The metropolitan prefecture of the Chang’an region; named with Luozhou in the statute defining the censors’ patrol-bounds. Standard.

洛州.note: The prefecture of the eastern capital, Luoyang; named with Yongzhou in the quoted statute. Standard.

范阳.note: A Tang frontier command (northeast, about modern Beijing), one of the ten military-commissioner circuits with a resident-agent courtyard in Pingkang Ward. Standard.

平卢.note: A Tang frontier command (the northeast, toward Liaoning), one of the ten military-commissioner circuits. Standard.

朔方.note: A Tang frontier command on the northern Ordos frontier (Wang Zhongsi’s command); its resident-agent courtyard first reported the Türk incursion. Standard.

河西.note: A Tang frontier command of the Gansu corridor, one of the ten military-commissioner circuits. Standard.

安西.note: The Protectorate-General of Anxi in the Western Regions (the Tarim), one of the ten frontier commands. Standard.

北庭.note: The Protectorate-General of Beiting, north of the Tianshan, one of the ten frontier commands. Standard.

陇右.note: A Tang frontier command west of the Long Mountains toward Kokonor, one of the ten military-commissioner circuits. Standard.

剑南.note: A Tang frontier command in the southwest (about modern Sichuan), one of the ten military-commissioner circuits. Standard.

岭南五府.note: The Lingnan Five-Prefectures command in the far south (the historical 岭南五府经略使), counted as the tenth of the ten frontier commands with a courtyard in Pingkang Ward. Rendered ‘the Lingnan Five Prefectures’; cf. Lingnan.

宣阳坊.note: A ward east of the Vermilion Bird Avenue; the assassin Liu Shiqi’s escort-cart is ambushed at the Xuanyang-Changxing crossroads.

永乐坊.note: A ward on the route the escort-cart takes toward Pingkang Ward; it has just passed Yongle Ward when Zhang Xiaojing reaches the firepoint.

天竺.note: The Tang name for India (from Sanskrit Sindhu); source of the sal trees transplanted into Long Bo’s courtyard. Standard identification.

波斯.note: Sasanian Persia, whose royal house Yisi claims; officially the Nestorian church was styled the ‘Persian Temple’ (波斯寺) until it was recognized as coming from Daqin. Standard English form.

管仲祠.note: A ruined shrine to Guan Zhong in Pingkang Ward, patron of the pleasure quarter; next door stands the Shouzhuolang’s bookshop. Rendered literally.

花萼相辉楼.note: ‘The Tower Where the Blossoms and Their Calyxes Shine on One Another,’ one of the two great towers in the southwest of the Xingqing Palace, its name a figure for brotherly love; a historical structure. Romanized to match the Qinzheng Wuben Tower.

拱月桥.note: A bridge over the Longshou Canal at the Anxing–Chongren crossroads, a fine vantage for lantern-viewing; the name is descriptive (‘arched like the moon’), so rendered by sense.

兴庆坊.note: The ward that had been Xuanzong’s residence before his accession, later expanded into the Xingqing Palace. Standard.

永嘉坊.note: A ward of Chang’an, half of which was taken to enlarge Xingqing Ward. Standard.

胜业坊.note: A ward of Chang’an, half of which was taken to enlarge Xingqing Ward. Standard.

道业坊.note: One of the three wards (with Yongjia and Shengye) half of which was taken to enlarge Xingqing Ward. Pinyin of the source’s form.

太极宫.note: The original main palace of Tang Chang’an, in the north of the city; with the Daming Palace, one of the three great palace-complexes. Standard.

南内.note: By-name for the Xingqing Palace, so called for its position relative to the Taiji (‘Western Interior’) and Daming (‘Eastern Interior’) palaces. Rendered by sense.

春名门.note: A gate in the east wall of Chang’an, near the Xingqing Palace; the standard form is 春明门, and the source’s 春名门 has the same reading. Standard.

道政坊.note: A ward on the south side of the Xingqing Palace’s south plaza; Zhang Xiaojing enters it to reach the underground water-channel beneath the Longshou Canal.

出云.note: Izumo, an old province on the Japan Sea coast of Japan; Chao Fen’s birthplace. Standard form.

端门.note: The southern gate of the imperial city of Luoyang, before which Wu Zetian’s Tianshu column stood. Standard identification.

金明门.note: One of the gates below the Qinzheng Wuben Tower, held by the Longwu Army on the festival night.

初阳门.note: One of the gates below the Qinzheng Wuben Tower, held by the Longwu Army on the festival night.

通阳门.note: One of the gates below the Qinzheng Wuben Tower, held by the Longwu Army on the festival night.

安西都护府.note: The Tang Protectorate-General of Anxi, governing the Western Regions from its seat at Kucha; 都护府 rendered ‘the Protectorate’ per Hucker.

广武.note: A Tang county in the Lanzhou region (near modern Yongdeng, Gansu); Xiao Gui’s sister’s home, where his family was destroyed. Pinyin.

灵武.note: A frontier town in the Guannei region (modern Lingwu, Ningxia); Xiao Gui and Yuchang shelter in a garrison-town nearby. Pinyin.

兰州.note: Prefecture and Area Command on the upper Yellow River (modern Lanzhou, Gansu). Pinyin.

阴山.note: The Yinshan range across the northern steppe frontier, where Li Jing broke the Eastern Türks in 630. Rendered ‘the Yin Mountains.’

沙雁.note: A place named in the flashback as lying behind the beacon-fort, between it and Balhuan/Kucha; not securely identified. Provisional pinyin.

南山.note: The Zhongnan range 终南山 south of Chang’an; the home of the old charcoal-seller, as in Bai Juyi’s ballad. Rendered ‘the Southern Mountains.’

越州.note: A prefecture of the southeast, about modern Shaoxing in Zhejiang. Pinyin.

营州.note: A northeastern frontier prefecture, about modern Chaoyang in Liaoning; the seat of An Lushan’s Pinglu command. Pinyin.

河北.note: The region north of the Yellow River; in Tang usage the northeastern circuit, not the modern province of the same name. Pinyin.

林邑.note: Champa (Lâm Ấp), the Cham kingdom of the central Vietnamese coast, a source of aromatics such as borneol. Pinyin of the Tang name.

青云观.note: A Daoist abbey named in passing (a priest of it is quoted). Rendered like Mystic Abbey with 观 = ‘Abbey’; 青云 kept in pinyin.

武威.note: The name of a lantern-chamber (its theme, Duke Li of Wei breaking the Yin Mountains), next to the Tangdi chamber. Kept in pinyin like Tangdi.

龙池.note: The Dragon Pool at the heart of the Xingqing Palace gardens; deep and broad enough for pleasure-boats, ringed by the palace pavilions. Historically the pool on the grounds of Xuanzong’s princely residence before his accession. Pinyin.

摘星殿.note: The seven-story upper hall of the Qinzheng Wuben Tower, from whose outward terrace the Lantern-Crown Red Tally casts the lighting-candle. Literal rendering of “pluck the stars.”

龙亭.note: One of the pavilions rising along the Longchi in the Xingqing Palace gardens. Literal.

灵官阁.note: A level of the Mystic Abbey beneath the lantern-tower where Li Bi was held captive (ch16). Pinyin + “loft.”

长乐坊.note: A ward in the northeastern city near the Xingqing Palace, holding the Ten Kings’ Residence where the heir apparent dwelt. Written 长乐; falls together in pinyin with the southeastern 常乐坊 (also ‘Changle Ward’), a distinction footnoted at first appearance.

修行坊.note: A ward in the southeastern city, site of the Tongfa Temple and its pagoda.

安国寺.note: A great Chang’an monastery; the Ten Kings’ Residence lay in the annexed park-city to its east.

十王宅.note: The walled compound near the Daming Palace where Xuanzong housed his adult sons, the heir apparent among them, under close watch.

终南山.note: The range south of Chang’an (the same range called 南山, the Southern Mountains, in verse); source of the fantastic garden-stones of the Longchi rockery.

通法寺.note: A temple in Xiuxing Ward, its tall pagoda a landmark of the southern city.

遮沟.note: The Chang’an residents’ nickname (遮沟, lit. ‘screened gully’) for the valley-road running between the eastern city wall and the high slope of the Leyou Plateau; the source glosses the name in the text.

隆庆坊.note: The former Wannian-County ward beside the well-fed marsh that became the Longchi; absorbed into the Xingqing Palace.

隆庆池.note: The marsh-pool of Longqing Ward, renamed the Longchi (‘Dragon Pool’) on Xuanzong’s accession as a token of the dragon’s rising.

沉香亭.note: The ‘Aloeswood Pavilion’ on the bank of the Longchi within the Xingqing Palace gardens.

平康坊.note: A ward of the eastern capital; its Pingkang Quarter (平康里) was the famed courtesans’ district.

东宫.note: The residence and establishment of the heir apparent; by metonymy the heir apparent himself.

玄武门.note: The northern palace gate of the Tang capital, scene of the coup of 626; here invoked for the ‘kin-slaying’ strain in the Li house.

观音寺.note: A small temple in Jinggong Ward with a famous jade Guanyin, bound to Prince Yong through his mother the Lady Guo; site of the polo-field flashback. ch20.

华清池.note: The hot-spring pool at Mount Li east of Chang’an, famed for the bathing of Xuanzong and Yang Guifei (Bai Juyi, ‘Song of Everlasting Regret’). ch20.

河间.note: A prefecture in Hebei; home of the Pifu Wu Guiyi. ch20.

金城.note: A commandery about modern Lanzhou; home of the Pifu Mo Wa’er. ch20.

河南县.note: A metropolitan county at Luoyang; home of the Pifu Suo Fahui. ch20.

疾陵城.note: A city of the far Western Regions (Zaranj, in Sistan), seat of the Tang Persian Governorate set up for the exiled Sasanian prince Peroz. Home of the old artisan who built the Yaluoshan into the tower.

陇西.note: A commandery west of the Long mountains (in modern Gansu); ancestral seat of the Li clan, including the imperial house and Li Linfu.

太极殿.note: The main audience hall of the Taiji Palace (the ‘Western Precinct’), where the earliest Tang emperors held court before the Daming and Xingqing palaces were built.

永安宫.note: The palace Taizong raised east of the Taiji Hall (the ‘Eastern Precinct’), later renamed the Daming Palace.

望仙门.note: A gate on the southern wall of the Daming Palace; the northern terminus of the walled corridor.

通化门.note: A gate in Chang’an’s eastern outer rampart, passed by the walled corridor on its way to the Xingqing Palace.

曲江.note: The scenic Qujiang district and pool in Chang’an’s southeast, southern terminus of the extended walled corridor; also written 曲江池, the Qujiang Pool.

朱雀街.note: Short form of 朱雀大街, Chang’an’s central north–south boulevard.

贞顺武皇后庙.en: the Temple of Empress Wu Zhenshun
贞顺武皇后庙.note: The shrine to Consort Wu in Anye Ward, the ward’s most famous building.

统万城.note: Helian Bobo’s Xia capital (built from 413) on the Ordos steppe; a byword for indestructibly hard rammed-earth walls, to which the outer rampart of Chang’an is compared. Pinyin + ‘City’.

兴化坊.note: A residential ward southeast of Guangde Ward, holding two watchtowers set catty-corner; where the runner-traitor ambushes Yao Runeng. Pinyin + ‘Ward’ (as the other 坊).

永崇坊.note: A residential ward in the eastern half of Chang’an, near the Yanxing Gate; the site of an abandoned mercy-release pond said to be haunted by a fox-spirit. Pinyin.

靖安坊.note: A ward in the eastern city marking a dividing line across Wannian County; site of Feng Dalun’s Yixiang Pavilion. Shares its two characters 靖安 (‘pacify and secure’) with the Jing’an Bureau (靖安司), an irony the text notes. Pinyin.

涪州.note: A prefecture on the Yangzi in the east of modern Chongqing (about modern Fuling); in later tradition the source of the fresh lychees rushed to Yang Guifei. Some 2,000 li from Chang’an. Pinyin.

子午谷.note: The northern mouth of the Ziwu Road, a route through the Qinling Mountains south of Chang’an; the post-road by which the lychee courier’s horse reaches the capital. Pinyin.

户县.note: A county southwest of Chang’an (modern Huyi District, Xi’an), at the northern foot of the Qinling range. Pinyin.

柳京.note: A byname of Xuanping Ward on the Leyou Plateau, the willow-thickest quarter of Chang’an, where He Zhizhang’s residence stood. Rendered literally. ch24.

山阴.note: He Zhizhang’s native place (in modern Shaoxing, Zhejiang), to which he retired in 744.

江陵.note: A city on the Yangzi (modern Jingzhou, Hubei); seat of Prince Yong’s power during the rebellion.

蜀中.note: The Shu region (modern Sichuan), to which Xuanzong fled in 756. Rendered ‘Shu.’

太原.note: The great northern city and military headquarters (modern Taiyuan, Shanxi); Wang Zhongsi held its command.

马嵬坡.note: The post-station west of Chang’an (马嵬驿) where the 756 mutiny forced the deaths of Yang Guozhong and Yang Guifei. Rendered ‘Mawei Slope.’

华阴.note: A county at the foot of Mount Hua (modern Huayin, Shaanxi); Yao Runeng is styled its commandant.

西安.note: The modern city on the site of Tang Chang’an, where the author did field research. Standard form.

长信.note: A Han palace (长信宫) associated with the neglected consort Ban Jieyu; invoked in Wang Yunxiu’s dying words as a byword for a consort’s fate written into history.

昭阳.note: A Han palace hall (昭阳殿) associated with the favorite Zhao Feiyan; paired with Changxin in Wang Yunxiu’s allusion.

上元节.note: The fifteenth night of the first lunar month (Shangyuan), when the curfew was lifted and the city was lit with lanterns; here its eve, the fourteenth.

时辰.note: One of the twelve shichen into which the traditional day was divided, each equal to two modern hours and named for one of the twelve earthly branches / zodiac animals. Rendered ‘double-hour’ in the prose.

望楼.note: The tall signal towers standing in every ward, from which watchmen relay messages by flag in daylight and lantern by night.

武侯.note: The watch-constables who man the watchtowers and street posts. Rendered ‘constable’ throughout.

不良帅.note: The head of a county’s buliang, the plainclothes thief-catchers; the deputy to the constable-magistrate in charge of policing. Rendered with the loanword buliang.

不良人.note: Tang plainclothes thief-catchers and informants who policed the wards under the buliang chief.

县尉.note: The county-level official responsible for law enforcement and public order, directly supervising the buliang chief. Not the county magistrate (县令, xiànlìng), who was the head of the county administration.

狼卫.note: The khagan’s most feared elite—cruel, cunning, and fanatically loyal; the ‘wolves’ the Jing’an Bureau hunts.

突厥.note: The Turkic people of the Second Turkic Khaganate. ‘Türk’ per standard Turkological usage.

粟特.note: The Iranian merchant people of Central Asia who dominated Silk Road trade. Standard.

过所.note: The official guosuo permit required to move goods and persons through the empire’s checkpoints.

阙勒霍多.note: A Turkic phrase the text glosses in part: que-le as something near a nine-layered blood-hell, huo-duo as being turned to dust—at once a curse and a legendary beast of destruction. Transliteration mine, from the novel’s Chinese characters.

银鱼袋.note: A fish-shaped tally in a pouch worn at the belt as a badge of official rank; gold for the highest, silver below. Granting one above a man’s grade signaled special imperial favor.

待诏翰林.note: A scholar attached to the emperor’s Hanlin establishment, awaiting summons; a prestigious but nominally leisured post.

圣人.note: A Tang court term of address for the reigning emperor (here Xuanzong). Rendered ‘the Sage.’

明光铠.note: Mingguang plate armor, named for the polished discs at the breast that flashed in the light; heavy, which nearly drowns Cui Qi.

横刀.note: The hengdao, the standard single-edged Tang military saber worn at the waist.

天宝.note: The third and last reign-era of Emperor Xuanzong (742–756); its years were counted with the word zai rather than nian. Tianbao 3 = 744 CE. Standard.

开元.note: Xuanzong’s preceding reign-era (713–741), remembered as the high noon of Tang prosperity. Standard.

熊火帮.note: A gang of idle ruffians terrorizing Wannian County, several hundred strong.

西府店.note: A gold-and-silver shop and currency exchange in the West Market, owned by a Sogdian of Kang.

元来行.note: A Kashgar merchant’s enterprise dealing in large-scale livestock, with ties to the steppe.

障刀.note: A short, light combat blade suited for close quarters, lighter than the standard hengdao saber.

寸弩.note: A small, concealable crossbow issued by the Jing’an Bureau; single-shot, requiring manual re-cocking.

烟丸.note: A signaling device containing white phosphorus, sulfur, and other combustibles; ignites in the wind and produces colored smoke.

祆教.note: The Iranian fire-religion, widespread in Central Asia and the Türk steppe. Tang Chang’an had temples for its foreign-born adherents. Standard identification.

祆正.note: The government-appointed head of a Zoroastrian temple, equivalent to the abbot of a Chinese monastery.

景教.note: The Church of the East (Nestorian Christianity) as known in Tang China. The Right Shad disguises himself as a Nestorian priest. Standard identification.

五尊阎罗.note: Zhang Xiaojing’s street name in Wannian County, for the five demons he embodies: vicious, venomous, ruthless, stubborn, and pitiless.

红拂.note: A legendary Tang figure from the romance The Tale of the Curly-Bearded Hero: a maidservant who eloped with a hero. Li Bi teases Tanqi with the allusion. Standard.

闻记香铺.note: Wen Ran’s family incense shop, located in Dunyi Ward.

玉真观.note: A high-end face-cream shop in the West Market’s southeast quarter, run by a wealthy foreign proprietor.

昆仑奴.note: Tang term for dark-skinned servants brought from the southern seas and beyond, stock figures of Tang tales. Standard.

僧祇奴.note: A slave from the Zanj (East African) coast; Old Ge’s origin. Standard identification (Schafer, The Golden Peaches of Samarkand).

马兹达.note: Ahura Mazda, the supreme god of Zoroastrianism; the novel transliterates the name 马兹达. Standard.

饮中八仙.en: the Eight Immortals of the Wine Cup
饮中八仙.note: The eight Tang tipplers of Du Fu’s poem Song of the Eight Immortals of the Wine Cup.

大案牍术.en: the art of the Great Archive
大案牍术.note: Xu Bin’s method of cross-referencing the capital’s mass of paper records to deduce hidden facts; introduced in ch02 as the art of the ‘Great Archive.’

遛马.note: Pingkang-Quarter cant: to take a courtesan out on an excursion; paired with 留沐 (‘staying to bathe’), lodging the night. The text glosses both.

一曲.note: The northern of the Pingkang Quarter’s three lanes (曲), also called the North Lane (北曲); the humblest. 中曲 = the Middle Lane, 南曲 = the South Lane.

奚车.note: A railed, canopy-less cart of the Xi (奚) people of the northeast steppe, drawn here by camels; a fashionable steppe novelty.

三勒浆.note: A Tang cordial of Persian origin, made from three fruits (三勒); a holiday drink.

三辅.note: The three metropolitan commanderies around the capital (a Han-era term for the Chang’an region); here loosely ‘the capital region.’

幞头.note: The soft cloth head-wrap or cap worn by Tang men over a headcloth.

思恩客.note: A wooden tally issued only to a courtesan-house’s regular patrons in the Pingkang Quarter, admitting the bearer straight behind the curtains.

投名状.note: The bandit’s pledge of allegiance sealed by a killing, proving the newcomer has burned his bridges. Rendered ‘oath-token of blood.’ Footnoted at first appearance (ch03).

九关鼓.note: The Jing’an Bureau’s alarm-drum: sounded from a ward’s watchtower, it shuts that ward and the eight around it and barricades the sixteen crossroads between the nine wards. Rendered ‘Nine-Gate Drum.’

五坊.note: The five imperial establishments rearing the emperor’s hunting eagles, gyrfalcons, hawks, sparrowhawks, and hounds, under the Xuanhui Court; source of the notorious mid-Tang ‘Five Kennels boys’ (五坊小儿). Attested Tang institution.

狗坊.note: The hound establishment among the Five Kennels; Zhang Xiaojing hopes to borrow keen-nosed dogs from it to track the Türks by scent.

节度使.note: The regional military governor of a Tang frontier command; Wang Zhongsi holds this office (of Shuofang), so 王节度 is rendered ‘the military commissioner Wang.’

铸肉钱.note: A Türk torture the text self-glosses: shaving off coin-sized rounds of flesh (the size of a copper cash) from a non-fatal spot such as the armpit, painful enough to make a prisoner confess to anything.

击鞠.note: The Tang mounted ball game (jiju, also 马球 maqiu), played with a crescent-headed mallet; a passion of the Tang court and nobility. Rendered ‘polo.’

大理评事.en: Evaluator of the Court of Judicial Review
大理评事.note: A junior judicial officer (评事, Evaluator) of the Court of Judicial Review, of the eighth rank, who deliberated on cases and rectified the statutes. Rendering per C. O. Hucker.

新罗.note: The Korean kingdom of Silla; Silla maidservants (新罗婢) were prized in Tang noble households. Standard identification.

邸报.note: The official gazette circulating court news and appointments; Feng Dalun searches his memory of the Tianbao gazettes. Rendered ‘the Tianbao gazette’ for 天宝邸报.

病坊.note: A charitable Tang institution sheltering and treating the sick and destitute (the beitian / bingfang almshouses, run under Buddhist auspices). Rendered ‘infirmary.’

雪饮子.note: A chilled sweet drink, a luxury; Prince Yong sips one court-side. Rendered ‘snow-cordial.’

节级.note: A low ranking jailer-officer; the death-cell warder (死牢节级) of the Chang’an County yamen who kept Zhang Xiaojing. Rendered ‘warder.’

石脂.note: The novel’s shizhi (literally ‘stone-grease’), the black oil that seeps from rock crevices in the northwest: petroleum/naphtha, smuggled in declared as ink-stock. Rendered ‘rock-oil.’

猛火.note: The army’s name (menghuo) for the incendiary made from refined rock-oil, which clings burning to a body and cannot be put out. Rendered ‘fierce-fire.’

猛火雷.note: The sealed-jar bomb of treated rock-oil that bursts with a thunderclap (menghuo lei). Rendered ‘fierce-fire thunder.’

延墨.note: The famous ink of Yanzhou, made from the soot of burning rock-oil; the cover under which the Türks declare their cargo.

火浣布.note: Asbestos cloth, known in China as huohuanbu, ‘fire-washed cloth,’ which takes no harm from flame; the constables’ fire-fighting gear. Rendered ‘fire-proof cloth.’

过龙槛.note: The notched stone threshold at a market or ward gate that admits only carts of a fixed wheel-gauge (five chi three cun for the two markets, four chi elsewhere). Rendered ‘dragon-sill.’

缚索.note: The oxsinew capture-cord carried by the capital’s buliang men, flicked out from the wrist to snare a fugitive. Rendered ‘binding-cord.’

唐韵.note: The Tang Yun, Sun Mian’s revised rhyme-dictionary; the watchtowers’ rhyme-code indexes characters by its scroll, rhyme, and position. Historical; rendered ‘the Tang Rhymes.’

蜥皮鼓.note: A drum headed with lizard-skin, imported from Persia and reserved for the Jing’an Bureau’s low, far-carrying signal-beats. Rendered literally.

假节望楼.note: The Jing’an Bureau’s grant of tally-authority (jiajie) over all watchtowers to one field commander, who then receives and directs their dispatches directly. Rendered ‘commissioning the watchtowers.’

石经幢.note: A dharani-pillar (jingchuang): a tall polygonal stone column inscribed with Buddhist scripture, raised at vital sites and here also gauging the canal’s depth. Rendered ‘stone sutra-pillar.’

仪制令.note: The Tang Yizhi ling, the code of ceremonial that included the road-priority rule ‘the low give way to the high, the departing to the coming.’ Historical; rendered ‘the Statutes of Ceremonial.’

参军.note: An canjun (administrative aide) on the staff of a guard command or prefecture. Rendered ‘adjutant.’

云麾将军.note: A Tang prestige title (sanguan) of the junior third rank, the highest military honorific below the four Grand Generals; Wang Zhongsi holds it. Rendering per C. O. Hucker.

棠棣集.note: Adjutant Zhao’s little vanity-printed book of verse; 棠棣 (the flowering cherry of the Book of Songs) is a byword for brotherly affection.

郎官清.note: A noted clear wine of the Toad Barrow in Changle Ward. Rendered ‘the Langguan Clear.’

帷帽.note: A wide-brimmed hat with a hanging veil of gauze, worn by Tang women out of doors to screen the face. Rendered ‘curtained hat.’

李花玉佩.note: A palm-sized white-jade pendant carved as a spray of plum blossom, a gift from Li Heng to Li Bi. The surname Li (李) is written with the character for the plum tree, so a plum-blossom (李花) token stands for the Li imperial clan—which lets it pass as Li Linfu’s. Rendered ‘plum-blossom jade.’

卢舍那.note: Locana (Vairocana), the cosmic ‘Resplendent’ Buddha; a Locana image stands in the Cibei Temple hut. Standard Buddhological form.

乙计划.note: The contingency plans are labeled by the heavenly stems 甲/乙/丙, rendered as Plan A / Plan B / Plan C; the watchtower semaphore that signals Plan 乙 is rendered ‘B.’

素油子.note: A Lantern-Festival street food of Chang’an: balls of wet dough deep-fried in oil. Rendered ‘plain-oil fritters.’

十字莲花.note: The emblem the dying Cao Poyan names: in Tang Nestorian art a cross rising from a lotus (as atop the 781 Xi’an Stele), fusing the Christian cross with the Buddhist lotus. Rendered ‘the cross-and-lotus.’

景寺.note: A temple of the Nestorian faith (景教); rendered ‘Nestorian temple,’ consistent with 景教 = ‘Nestorian.’

景僧.note: A cleric of the Nestorian church; the source uses the Buddhist-flavored 僧. Rendered ‘Nestorian monk.’

三夷教.note: The Tang grouping of the three Western faiths of the resident foreign communities: Zoroastrianism (祆), Manichaeism (摩尼), and Nestorian Christianity (景). Rendered ‘the Three Foreign Religions.’

摩尼.note: The dualist religion founded by the prophet Mani; one of the Three Foreign Religions of Tang Chang’an. 摩尼庙 = ‘Manichaean temple.’ Standard identification.

苫国.note: The Tang name (from Arabic al-Shām) for Syria and the Levant, a homeland of some Nestorian believers. Standard identification.

执事.note: The temple office Yisi holds; rendered by its Christian equivalent, ‘deacon.’

大主教.note: The head of the Nestorian church in Chang’an, of a standing like the Zoroastrians’ Great Sabao. Rendered ‘archbishop.’

度牒.note: The official certificate (dudie) licensing a monk or priest; the Bureau checks these to vet the clergy of a temple.

告解室.note: The Nestorian temple’s confessional (告解 = confession), sealed from sight and sound; Yisi locks Zhang and Tanqi inside it. Rendered ‘the confession room.’

惜字令.en: the Ordinance to Cherish Written Characters
惜字令.note: An injunction (the custom of jing xi zizhi, revering paper that bears writing) forbidding the use of written-on paper in the privy; Registrar Pang pleads it as his cover. Rendered by sense.

降神芸香.note: A made-to-order incense (芸香 = rue) the Wang household favors, by whose scent Zhang Xiaojing claims to trace Wang Yunxiu. Rendered by sense.

贞观.note: The reign-era of Emperor Taizong (627–649); Alopen reached Chang’an in its ninth year, 635. Standard.

陌刀.note: The long two-handed anti-cavalry saber of the Tang army; used here only as a metaphor for Zhang Xiaojing’s cutting words. Rendered by the loanword modao.

摩羯.note: The makara, an Indian sea-monster motif that entered Tang decorative art; the Right Shad keeps a makara-shaped wine-pot. Standard.

录事.note: A record-keeping officer (lushi); rendered ‘registrar’ to keep it distinct from 主事, ‘recorder’ (Xu Bin’s post).

蚍蜉.note: The name Long Bo gives his organization: pifu (蚍蜉) is a large ant, and the word invokes Han Yu’s line 蚍蜉撼大树 (‘ants that would shake a great tree’), which Long Bo turns into a boast. Kept as the transliteration ‘the Pifu’ so the allusion, footnoted at first appearance, can carry through.

唧筒.note: A bamboo piston-syringe (jitong): a tube with a nozzle and a cotton-wrapped rod, made to draw water in and squirt it out. Nominally a fire-fighting tool, the Pifu use it to spray rock-oil. Rendered ‘squirt-pump.’

离丧铃.note: A lead-weighted blue-and-white bell (lisang ling, ‘the bell of bereavement’) hung outside a cart rushing a gravely ill patient to an infirmary; its distinctive toll warns crowds to clear the way and avoid the ill luck. Rendered by sense.

獬豸.note: A one-horned mythical beast able to tell right from wrong, which gores the guilty; the emblem of law and of the Tang censors and judges. Cui Qi’s family carries a jade one. Standard sinological form; footnoted at first appearance.

胡旋舞.note: The huxuan dance, a fast spinning dance from Sogdiana and the Western Regions, a craze of Tang Chang’an; rendered ‘the Sogdian Whirl.’ The deputy squad-leader turns it into a cruel taunt as his victims burn. Footnoted at first appearance.

守捉城.note: A Tang frontier garrison-post (shouzhuo): a small walled camp of border troops, below an ‘army’ (军) in scale, self-governing and little regarded by the court. The word gives the Shouzhuolang their name. Rendered ‘garrison-town.’

留后院.note: The capital establishment (liuhou yuan) that a frontier military commissioner kept in Chang’an—in Pingkang Ward—to manage his affairs at court and serve, unofficially, as his intelligence-post and eyes and ears. Rendered ‘resident-agent courtyard.’

端公.note: The off-duty form of address for an Attendant Censor (侍御史). Yuan Zai flatters Ji Wen, a mere Palace Censor (properly ‘Vice-Duan’), by styling him a rank higher. Kept as the transliteration.

副端.note: The off-duty form of address proper to a Palace Censor (殿中侍御史), a rank below ‘Duangong.’ Rendered ‘Vice-Duan’ to keep the ‘Duan’ that carries the flattery.

殿中侍御史.note: A censor of the Palace Bureau of the Censorate, of the seventh rank, holding the commissions of the Left and Right Patrols over the two capitals; Ji Wen’s office. Rendering per C. O. Hucker.

侍御史.note: An investigating censor of the Censorate, a rank above the Palace Censor; addressed off duty as ‘Duangong.’ Rendering per C. O. Hucker.

左巡使.note: One of the two patrol commissions (左巡/右巡) held by a Palace Censor, charged with unlawful matters within the capital city (the Right Patrol taking those without). Rendered ‘Commissioner of the Left Patrol.’

拔灯.note: The Lantern-Festival parade troupes (badeng), ‘not lanterns at all’ but singers and dancers on great carts chosen by the provinces and sent to the capital; they converge before the Xingqing Palace at the fourth watch. Rendered ‘the lantern-floats.’

灯顶红筹.note: The title given the most acclaimed of the lantern-float performers, permitted to mount the Qinzheng Wuben Tower and light the greatest lantern-tower beside the emperor. Rendered by sense.

牧护歌.note: An old folk tune of the Qishan country, sung over the blessing-wine after a sacrifice; the melody Tanqi hums. A real Tang quzi tune-title; kept as the transliteration ‘the Muhu song.’

胡笳.note: The hujia, a double-reed pipe of the northern nomads, its wailing note a stock image of frontier sorrow in Tang verse; the subject of Cen Shen’s poem. Rendered ‘the nomad reed-pipe.’

大唐六典.note: The Tang Liudian (the ‘Six Statutes of the Great Tang’), the great administrative code of the Kaiyuan era; Yuan Zai reads out its article on the Palace Censors. Historical; kept as the transliteration.

百官格.note: A Tang legal compilation of regulations on the offices (Baiguan ge), quoted here on the censors’ patrol-bounds and monthly circuit. Rendered by sense.

神龙.note: The reign-era (705–707) of the restored Emperor Zhongzong, opened by the coup that ended Wu Zetian’s Zhou; the setting of the Zhou Lizhen / Huan Yanfan atrocity. Standard.

都护府.note: A Tang protectorate-general governing a frontier region; here the Western Regions command whose reward Wen Wuji brought home on retiring. Rendering per C. O. Hucker.

火点.note: Shouzhuolang cant (火点, ‘fire-point’) for a contact-point through which their commissions are handed out; Liu’s Bookshop is one. The text glosses the word as it introduces it. Rendered ‘firepoint.’

火师.note: The Shouzhuolang operative who runs a firepoint (火师, ‘fire-master’); the true one here is found murdered and impersonated. Rendered ‘firemaster,’ keeping the ‘fire’ of 火点/firepoint.
