自雨亭.note: A real Tang cooling device (自雨亭, ‘self-raining pavilion’): water raised to the roof and let fall from the eaves as a curtain to cool the air in summer. Long Bo’s stands in his courtyard. Rendered by sense; footnoted at first appearance.

春江花月夜.en: A Moonlit Night on the Spring River
春江花月夜.note: The famous early-Tang poem by Zhang Ruoxu (张若虚); the Shouzhuolang use its lines as call-and-response passwords. Rendered by an English title; footnoted at first appearance.

苏合香.note: An aromatic resin (苏合香) imported into Tang China from the west, used in perfumes, incense, and medicine; the carriage-scent Tanqi smells. Rendered ‘storax’; footnoted at first appearance. See E. H. Schafer, The Golden Peaches of Samarkand.

灯轮.note: A waterwheel-shaped revolving lantern (灯轮) whose twelve zodiac panels turn with the current as a figure for the passing hours; Long Bo’s is the test-piece for the Que-le Huo-duo. Rendered ‘lantern-wheel.’

福寿禄三星.en: the Three Stars (Fortune, Longevity, and Rank)
福寿禄三星.note: The three star-gods of Chinese folk belief—Fu (fortune/blessing), Shou (longevity), and Lu (rank/emolument)—painted at the hub of the lantern-wheel. Rendered by name.

娑罗树.note: The sal tree (娑罗, Shorea robusta), native to India (天竺); costly transplants wrapped against the northern cold stand in Long Bo’s courtyard. Standard identification.

金桃.note: The famous ‘golden peaches’ (金桃) sent as tribute to the Tang court from Samarkand, a byword for rare foreign luxury; one of the exotic trees in Long Bo’s courtyard. Standard (E. H. Schafer titled his study of Tang exotica The Golden Peaches of Samarkand).

京兆尹.note: The prefect (尹) governing the metropolitan Jingzhao Prefecture of Chang’an; cf. the Jingzhao Prefecture (京兆府). Rendering per C. O. Hucker.

中书令.note: The Director of the Secretariat (中书省), the office through which Ji Wen’s appointment comes; here Li Linfu’s power. Rendered ‘the Secretariat Director,’ distinct from ‘the Secretariat’ (中书省). Rendering per C. O. Hucker.

番仆.note: The foreign menial servants (番仆) of the Bureau, sent to carry the warrant to every ward. Rendered ‘foreign servants.’

三羽令.note: A dispatch graded by feathers: one feather a routine order, two an express order, three (三羽) an emergency to be carried out at once. The text glosses the grades. Rendered ‘a three-feather order.’

惊夜灯.note: The bright lamp kept burning at a ward-corner constable-post through the night (惊夜灯). Rendered ‘night-alarm lamp.’

卍字纹.note: The Buddhist auspicious emblem 卍 (wan) used as a decorative fret on the requisitioned lanterns. Rendered ‘the wan-character motif.’

四望车.note: A stately carriage open to view on all four sides (四望 = ‘views on four sides’), used in noble processions; the vehicle in the chapter’s flash-forward vignette. Rendered descriptively.

甩霞舞.note: A fashionable dance in which the dancer flings out long ribbons of brocade that trace patterns in the air like flying rosy clouds (甩 = ‘fling,’ 霞 = ‘rosy cloud’). The source coins and glosses the name; rendered to keep the image.

绿矾油.note: Oil of green vitriol, that is sulfuric acid, distilled by the Daoist alchemists from ferrous sulfate (绿矾, green vitriol); it corrodes paper, wood, and skin. Yuchang carries it in a sleeve-pouch. Rendered literally.

跑窟.note: A cant term for the acrobatic art of scaling walls and running the eaves and rooftops of the city; Yisi’s specialty. Rendered literally.

麻搭.note: A fire-fighting tool: a long wooden pole with a great wad of coarse hemp bound at the tip, dipped in water or mud to beat out flames. Rendered ‘fire-mop’ (as in Chapter Six).

推事厅.note: A hall in the Jingzhao Prefecture’s offices set aside for the deliberating of cases (tuishi); Ji Wen commandeers it as his private office. Rendered by function.

架阁库.note: A repository for storing documents and files (jiage ku), sharing a roof-beam with the Deliberation Hall. Rendered by function.

设厅.note: The hall of a government office used for receptions and banquets; here pressed into service as the treatment area for the night’s injured. Rendered by function.

婆罗门戏.note: A comic mummer’s turn in Indian (‘Brahman’) style; 弄婆罗门 is to play such a part. Zhang Xiaojing’s painted disguise passes for such a player. Rendered by sense.

地藏菩萨.note: Ksitigarbha (Chinese Dizang), the bodhisattva who vowed to save the beings of the hells; see the note at his first mention. Standard Sanskrit form.

景尊.note: Nestorian term of reverence for the Lord (Christ/God); 景 is the ‘Luminous Teaching’ (景教). Rendered ‘the Luminous Lord.’

霓裳羽衣舞.note: ‘The Dance of the Rainbow Skirt and Feathered Robe,’ the most celebrated dance-suite of Xuanzong’s court; see the note at its first mention. Rendered in short form.

黄狮子舞.note: A lion-dance reserved as the Son of Heaven’s own dance (tianzi zhi wu), performed only on such an occasion. Rendered by sense.

通天冠.note: The tongtian guan (‘sky-reaching crown’), a ridged ceremonial crown worn by the emperor; here counted at twelve ridges. Romanized.

放生池.note: A temple pond where captive creatures are freed as an act of Buddhist merit. Rendered ‘mercy-release pond’ (as in Chapter Seven).

太上玄元大灯楼.note: The giant festival lantern-tower designed by Mao Shun before the Xingqing Palace, named for the honorific 太上玄元 conferred on Laozi; the Pifu turn it into a vast fierce-fire thunder. 太上玄元 kept as pinyin (a title), the rest rendered.

麒麟臂.note: A precision jointing-piece of hollow bamboo, saw-toothed at both ends so two interlock and turn, used to make the lantern-tower’s figures move; the Pifu pack them with rock-oil as bomblets. Named for the 麒麟 (qilin); rendered ‘qilin-arm.’

秦王破阵舞.en: the Dance of the Prince of Qin Breaking the Line
秦王破阵舞.note: A celebrated Tang martial dance-and-music piece (秦王破阵乐) glorifying the campaigns of the future Emperor Taizong while still Prince of Qin. Historical; rendered by sense.

凤尾车.note: A lantern-float cart fanned with thousands of colored feathers into a phoenix’s tail; Xu Hezi’s cart, which Zhang Xiaojing commandeers. Rendered literally.

春壶车.note: A lantern-float cart of Western-Regions style that challenges the phoenix-tail cart. Rendered literally.

天枢.note: The ‘Axis of Heaven,’ Wu Zetian’s great bronze commemorative column before the Duanmen Gate of Luoyang, cast by Mao Poluo. Historical; footnoted at first appearance. Kept as pinyin.

遣唐使.en: a Japanese embassy to the Tang
遣唐使.note: The official embassies Japan sent to Tang China (the kentōshi); Chao Fen and Chao Heng came to Chang’an with one. Rendered by sense.

七杀.note: The malefic ‘Seven Killings’ star of Chinese astrology, invoked for a berserk, death-dealing frenzy (七杀附体, ‘possessed by the Seven Killings’). Rendered literally.

尚灯监.note: The office (and its holder, Mao Shun) charged with the festival lantern-works; addressed 毛监, ‘Director Mao.’ Rendered ‘Director of Lanterns.’

卫尉少卿.en: Vice-Minister of the Court of the Imperial Regalia
卫尉少卿.note: A Tang office (少卿 of the 卫尉寺); Chao Heng’s post. Rendering per C. O. Hucker, A Dictionary of Official Titles in Imperial China.

尚方丞.en: Aide in the Directorate for Imperial Manufactories
尚方丞.note: A Tang office (丞 of the 尚方); Mao Poluo’s post under the Wu Zhou. Rendering per C. O. Hucker.

竹籍.note: The craftsman’s identity permit written on bamboo strips (name, appearance, native place, master-lineage, ward and shop, authorizations, with an officer’s countersignature), required to approach the lantern-tower; cf. 匠牒, ‘craftsman’s warrant.’

第八团.note: The 第八都护团, a garrison company of the Protectorate, three hundred strong at full muster, wiped out but for three men at the beacon-fort. Rendered ‘the Eighth Company.’

玄观.note: A Daoist abbey (guan); here the broad brick-and-stone base built up under the lantern-tower. Rendered ‘Mystic Abbey’ (first used ch14).

环首刀.note: The straight, ring-pommeled single-edged saber of the Han–Tang armies. Rendered ‘ring-pommeled saber.’

三清.note: The three highest Daoist deities. Rendered ‘the Three Pure Ones.’

十一曜.note: The eleven heavenly bodies of Tang astrology (sun, moon, five planets, and the four calculated points Rahu, Ketu, and the rest). Rendered ‘the Eleven Luminaries.’

八卦.note: The eight trigrams of the Yijing, used here both to set out the tripods and for divination. Rendered ‘the Eight Trigrams.’

四山五岳.en: the Four Peaks and Five Marchmounts
四山五岳.note: The four sacred Buddhist mountains and the five sacred marchmounts of China. Rendered ‘the Four Peaks and the Five Marchmounts.’

芸香.note: Rue (Ruta), long used to protect books and to scent; the hereditary craft of the Wen family. Rendered ‘rue-incense.’

新丰酒.note: The celebrated wine of Xinfeng, east of Chang’an, praised in Tang verse. Rendered ‘Xinfeng wine.’

棠棣.note: The name of a lantern-chamber, from the Shijing ode 常棣/棠棣 on brotherhood; the theme is fraternal love. Kept as pinyin, glossed in text.

飞骑尉.note: A Tang prestige-title (xun merit rank) awarded for service; Zhang Xiaojing’s carries him into a Ministry-of-War post. Rendering per Hucker.

转机.note: The fine-steel gear at the crown of Mystic Abbey’s roof that takes power from the water-wheels and drives the Tianshu; the point Zhang Xiaojing means to wreck. A project rendering.

水力宫.note: The underground chamber of six great water-wheels that powers the lantern-tower; 宫 rendered ‘Hall’ (not ‘Palace’) for this subterranean machine-room. A project rendering.

团结兵.note: Tang local self-defense levies (团结兵), raised for home-district garrison duty, distinct from the fubing militia and the frontier armies. Kept in pinyin with a gloss word.

柱国.note: An honorary merit-title (勋官) of high rank; 柱国子, ‘a son of a Pillar of State,’ claims descent from a holder. See C. O. Hucker, A Dictionary of Official Titles in Imperial China.

越骑.note: A designation for an elite cavalryman (lit. ‘leaping horse’), here a trooper under An Lushan’s Pinglu command. Kept in pinyin with a gloss word.

丁防.note: Able-bodied men (丁) levied for frontier garrison duty (防) in the border prefectures. A project rendering.

顶阁.note: The square upper chamber atop Mystic Abbey’s roof, housing the turning-gear at the tower’s base; the linchpin joining tower and Hydraulic Hall. A project rendering.

灯屋.note: One of the twenty-four rotating illuminated tableaux-rooms mounted around the outer ring of the Taishang Xuanyuan Lantern-Tower, each depicting a scene as it turns to the zenith and lights.

天枢层.note: The core level of the lantern-tower, built around the central Tianshu pillar; its broad revolving ring of boards cuts across the whole interior.

鹘喙.note: A narrow observation-hole jutting from the tower’s outer face, used by the craftsmen to true the turning-arms; named for its beak-narrow foothold and a falcon’s keen eye. Literal.

猛火油.note: The black, sticky refined petroleum packed into the qilin-arms (fierce-fire thunder); when its seal breaks it burns instead of bursting. Cf. 石脂 rock-oil, 猛火雷 fierce-fire thunder.

梨园.note: Xuanzong’s imperial music-and-dance academy; its performers passed through the Jinming Gate. Standard English form.

教坊.note: The Tang office and quarter for court musicians and performers (the Jiaofang).

弹指.note: A finger-snap (弹指), used through the book as a very short unit of elapsed time.

狻猊.note: The suanni, a lion-like beast of legend, one of the traditional ‘nine sons of the dragon’; here the form of the wooden cross-frame at the lantern-tower’s summit.

旋臂.note: The great rotating bamboo arms of the lantern-tower, each driving three lantern-chambers around the tower’s outer ring.

灯楼.note: The lantern-tower; in this book the Taishang Xuanyuan Lantern-Tower raised for the Lantern Festival.

七香车.note: A luxurious carriage scented with seven aromatics; here the Right Minister’s conveyance.

倒碑门.note: A ward-wall gate whose leaf, in opening, topples forward to lie flat on the ground like a fallen stele, hauled back up by iron chains; the source glosses the name.

药圃.note: The Eastern Palace’s medicinal-herb garden in Shengping Ward.

浑脱舞.note: A vigorous, tumbling Central-Asian dance popular in Tang; here a figure for the leaping of the flames.

唐隆政变.note: The coup of 710 that overthrew Empress Wei and restored Ruizong; see notes.

先天政变.note: The coup of 713 by which Xuanzong destroyed Princess Taiping’s faction; see notes.

通天梯.note: The grand suspended stairway of the Qinzheng Wuben Tower, hung in air and borne only at each turn by the tower-pillars; 通天 = ‘reaching to the sky.’ Rendered by sense.

邀风堂.note: The open, wall-less third floor of the Qinzheng Wuben Tower, a summer place to take the breeze; 邀风 = ‘to woo the wind.’ Rendered by sense.

天汉桥.note: A small bridge on the south of the Star-Plucking Hall joining it to an outer viewing-platform; 天汉 = the Milky Way (‘Sky River’). Rendered by sense.

移春槛.note: A Tang court device: a wheeled wood-walled planter-cart of earth and growing flowers, a movable garden. Recorded in the Kaiyuan Tianbao Yishi; footnoted at first appearance (ch19). Rendered by sense.

牵春绳.note: The hempen ropes strung from the suanni cross-frame at the lantern-tower’s summit to the palace wall, hung with colored gauze; 牵春 = ‘drawing the spring along.’ Rendered by sense.

靖安令.en: the Director of the Jing’an Bureau
靖安令.note: The head of the Jing’an Bureau (令 = director), a rank above the Deputy Director (司丞). He Zhizhang holds it; his gold-rimmed turtle-knob seal outranks the Deputy Director’s. Rendered by office.

太子文学.note: A tutorial-secretarial office in the Eastern Palace establishment (Hucker: ‘Litterateur’); held by Xue Yi. Rendered by office.

那伽花.note: An exotic bloom named in the flowerbeds of the Qinzheng Wuben Tower; 那伽 transliterates Sanskrit naga (serpent-spirit). Rendered by transliteration.

观音.note: Avalokitesvara, bodhisattva of compassion; the ‘Water-Dripping Guanyin’ (滴水观音) is the willow-and-vase form pouring sweet dew. ch20.

坤道.note: A woman ordained as a Daoist priest (坤 = the female principle); Taizhen appears in such robes. ch20.

来氏八法.en: the Eight Methods of the house of Lai
来氏八法.note: The eight named tortures the text ascribes to Lai Junchen (see ch10 note); the emetic method 万流归宗 is called the lightest. ch20.

万流归宗.en: All Streams Return to the Source
万流归宗.note: A named emetic torture (fish-mint and baiwei broth forced down, the mouth then stopped), the lightest of the Eight Methods of the house of Lai. ch20.

蹀躞带.note: A Tang leather utility belt hung with detachable straps and small tools; the Son of Heaven’s folding knife hangs from his. ch20.

鸱吻.note: The dragon-fish ridge-end ornament of Chinese roofs, a fire-warding water-charm. ch20 (see note).

楼内楼.note: Mao Shun’s hidden independent floor-load structure in the Qinzheng Wuben Tower, carrying weight through bracket-sets rather than corner-pillars; wrecking its junctures collapses the floors. ch20.

敛式斗拱.note: The compacted dougong bracket clusters that, with the attached turning-beams, transmit the floor-loads of the ‘tower within the tower.’ ch20.

附转梁.note: The load-transferring beams paired with the close-set bracket-sets in Mao Shun’s hidden support system. ch20.

拔灯红筹.note: The title and prize won by the year’s foremost lantern-float troupe (拔灯 + 红筹); its holder, a girl, is glimpsed in the flash-forward. ch20.

夹城.note: A concealed passage running within a doubled city wall, built so the emperor could move between his palaces unseen; here 夹城复道, the walled corridor. Historical.

复道.note: The covered/raised way running through the 夹城; often paired as 夹城复道, the walled corridor.

跸口.note: A widened bay set at intervals along the corridor where attendants could step aside and vehicles pass; bi is the clearing of the way before an imperial progress.

缒架.note: A windlass-and-basket rig on the city wall for hoisting a man or horse over when the gates were shut at night.

号旗.note: A flag on the wall-top used for signaling.

披帛.note: The long draped silk scarf worn over the shoulders and arms by Tang women of rank.

假披.note: An informal way of wearing the silk stole—looped loosely over one arm rather than round the neck—used in private among intimates; here Taizhen turns it into a weapon.

手实.note: A Tang self-declared register of a household’s persons and property; here the deed-record of a residence.

隐寄.note: The practice of buying property in a dependent’s or slave’s name to hide the true owner’s identity.

授宅推恩令.en: the Edict of Grace on the Bestowal of Residences
授宅推恩令.note: A decree restricting sale of the residences in the four wards flanking the Vermilion Bird Avenue to the imperial lineage and titled nobility. Novelistic.

象牙柄折刀.note: The Son of Heaven’s own folding knife, taken by Zhang Xiaojing in the Star-Plucking Hall and passed to Taizhen; a recurring prop through ch20–ch21.

城上郎.note: An officer set over a group of sentry posts on the city wall.

邀风阁.note: A source variant of 邀风堂 (the Wind-Wooing Hall), the open third floor of the Qinzheng Wuben Tower; rendered with the same decided form.

巽位.note: In the watchtower grid, the country around the great watchtower is divided into eight sectors named for the Eight Trigrams; the Xun (巽) trigram lies to the southeast. Pinyin for the trigram + ‘position’.

中元节.note: The fifteenth of the seventh lunar month, when the dead are honored and lanterns floated for them; here the source notes that its custom of water-lanterns for the departed has been carried over into the Lantern Festival (上元节). Conventional English name.

祖道庙.en: the roadside shrine of the god of journeys
祖道庙.note: A small shrine to the god of roads, standing on the highway outside the city gates, where travelers and those seeing them off made an offering for a safe journey (the rite of 祖). Descriptive rendering; the custom is footnoted at ch22.

风脚野驼.note: Aluoyue’s dreamed-of camel breed, prized for swiftness (‘wind-footed’). Literal rendering.

水灯.note: A small float—a board or sheet of oiled paper bearing a candle—set adrift (here, on the frozen moat) to ferry the dead; a Ghost-Festival custom carried into the Lantern Festival. Literal rendering.

应龙旗.note: The crimson, saw-toothed pennant of an imperial express courier; before it, even a strict gate-closure order is void. 应龙 (yinglong) is the winged ‘responding dragon’ of myth. Its seven teeth mark the seven days allowed for the delivery. Footnoted at first appearance (ch23).

山文甲.note: Tang lamellar armor whose plates are each shaped like the character 山 (‘mountain’), interlocking into a scaled surface. Rendered ‘mountain-pattern armor.’

迷幻香.note: A hallucinogenic incense of datura flower, hemp seed, and nutmeg that dulls the senses and raises illusions; Wen Ran’s weapon at the Yixiang Pavilion. Rendered ‘befuddling-incense’ (distinct from the fabled 迷魂香).

迷魂香.note: The legendary incense said to drop a man senseless at one whiff; the text has Wen Ran deny that any such thing exists. Rendered ‘soul-stealing incense.’

双陆.note: A Tang two-player race-game played with dice on a board, a relative of backgammon; a favorite pastime of the age. Rendered ‘double-sixes’. Footnoted at first appearance (ch04).

城门郎.note: The officer commanding the soldiers of a city gate (under the Gate Directorate); may move the guard-soldiers but does not hold the keys. Rendered ‘the gate-commander.’ The supervising 城门监 is ‘the Gate Inspectorate.’

监门.note: The gate-guard office (监门卫) that keeps the city-gate keys, deliberately separate from the gate-commander so no one man can both open and unlock a gate; its 门仆 are the ‘gate-servants’ who carry the keys. Rendered ‘the Gate Watch.’

鱼符.note: A Tang credential in the form of a bronze fish split into halves, matched to authenticate an official’s or courier’s identity and authority. Rendered ‘fish-tally.’

寄粜.note: A term the text glosses: court officials laundered large, unavowable transactions by entrusting a rich merchant—later a military commissioner’s resident-agent courtyard—to run the receipts and outlays through its own books, so that the true principal (the 寄粜人, the ‘consignment client’) stayed hidden. Literally 寄 ‘to consign’ + 粜 ‘to sell grain.’ Rendered ‘consignment-sale.’

太子宾客.note: A senior honorary post attached to the household of the heir apparent (Hucker: Adviser to the Heir Apparent / ‘Guest’); the office He Zhizhang held. Rendered by function.

翰林.note: A scholar of the Hanlin Academy (翰林院), the emperor’s inner circle of literary and drafting talent; Li Bi serves the Eastern Palace as one. Kept in pinyin, ‘Hanlin,’ with ‘academician.’

回纥.note: The Uyghur (Huihe) confederation that overran the last Türk remnant in 745 and became the Tang’s chief steppe ally. Standard form ‘Uyghur.’

采访使.note: A regional inspecting official of the Tang (Hucker: Surveillance Commissioner). 河北采访使 = Surveillance Commissioner of Hebei.

贵妃.note: The highest rank of imperial consort below the empress; Yang Yuhuan (Taizhen) was invested with it. Rendered ‘Noble Consort.’

太上皇.note: The honorific of an abdicated or superseded emperor; Xuanzong held it after 756. Rendered ‘Retired Emperor.’

客卿.note: An adviser serving without formal office; Li Bi’s chosen standing at Suzong’s court.

白衣宰相.note: ‘Chancellor in commoner’s white,’ the epithet for Li Bi, who guided policy while refusing office and rank.

宰相.note: The chief minister of the Tang; rendered ‘chancellor’ (distinct from the specific office 右相, the Right Minister).

邺县侯.note: Li Bi’s fief-title, conferred for his services under four reigns.

金紫光禄大夫.en: Grand Master of the Palace with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon
金紫光禄大夫.note: A senior prestige title of the Tang (Hucker). Held by the Nestorian Yisi.

节度副使.note: The deputy to a 节度使 (military commissioner); Yisi held it concurrently for Shuofang.

殿中监.note: Head of the Palace Administration (殿中省) (Hucker); Yisi held it on a probationary (试) basis.

紫袈裟.note: A purple monastic robe granted as an imperial honor to eminent clerics.

安史之乱.note: The rebellion of 755–763 led by An Lushan and Shi Siming that broke the High Tang; named 安史 for the two leaders, rendered ‘the An Lushan Rebellion’ as in the ch16 note.

大秦景教流行中国碑.en: the Stele of the Propagation in China of the Luminous Religion of Daqin
大秦景教流行中国碑.note: The Nestorian Stele of 781, erected by Yisi at the Daqin Temple in Chang’an and rediscovered in the Ming; a primary monument of Tang Christianity.

安禄山事迹.note: A real Tang work in three juan attributed to Yao Runeng; its Mawei passage names a Zhang Xiaojing, the seed of the novel.

刺客信条.note: The Ubisoft video-game series; a Zhihu question about setting one in China seeded the novel.

知乎.note: A Chinese question-and-answer website. Standard romanization.

24小时.note: The American real-time television series 24; its per-episode structure inspired the novel’s division into the half-shichen of one day.

靖安司丞.note: The 丞 (deputy) of the Jing’an Bureau; Li Bi’s office. Rendered ‘Deputy Director’ throughout.
